abstract: >-
  Simulation-based cutoff values for conditional item fit can be estimated by
  parametric bootstrapping and reported as an interval of a chosen width.
  Johansson (2025) recommended this over rule-of-thumb critical values but gave
  iteration guidance without accounting for the error rate that the interval
  width controls. This paper re-examines iterations and width against the
  familywise error rate (FWER), and compares FWER and false discovery rate
  control, in seven simulation studies with dichotomous and polytomous items.
  The interval width is shown to set the FWER of the interval rule jointly with
  the number of items. Bootstrap p-values with a Westfall-Young step-down target
  that error rate directly and detect more misfit than a width-matched interval.
  When all items fit, their FWER was at or slightly below the nominal level from
  400 iterations, and the small excess at fewer iterations came from how the
  statistics are studentized. Holm performed similarly once iterations cleared
  its floor, which grows with the number of items, while Benjamini-Hochberg
  flagged more fitting items. When some items misfit, every procedure exceeded
  its nominal rate at large samples, because misfit contaminates the total score
  that conditional fit is computed on. Conditional outfit was less powerful than
  infit throughout. Recommendations include flagging items on the Westfall-Young
  corrected p-value, using at least 400 iterations and 1000 to 2000 for a final
  analysis, reporting the interval as a descriptive band at width .95, and
  removing items one at a time. The methods are available in the R package
  `easyRasch2` and the jamovi module `easyRasch2jmv`.

# Introduction

Psychometric analysis often relies on rule-of-thumb critical values for interpreting fit metrics, but no fixed value or range can generalize across analyses, because the distribution of a fit statistic under a correctly fitting model depends on features of the data and the model, such as the sample size and the number of items [@muller_item_2020;@mcneish_direct_2024]. Johansson [-@johansson_detecting_2025] argued that such values should be replaced with simulation-based (parametric bootstrap) cutoffs tailored to the sample and items at hand, and evaluated this approach for conditional item infit [@muller_item_2020] through a series of simulation studies using the `easyRasch` R package [@easyrasch2024]. Infit with simulation-based cutoffs outperformed the item-restscore method [@kreiner_note_2011] with samples below 500 respondents, and the paper provided practical guidance on sample sizes, iterative item removal, and the number of bootstrap iterations. The present paper builds on that work and corrects parts of it.

The iteration guidance in Johansson [-@johansson_detecting_2025] recommended 100 bootstrap iterations for samples up to 250 respondents and 200 to 400 iterations for larger samples. That guidance was based on detection rates, since fewer iterations appeared to detect more misfit items with smaller samples. This paper shows that the apparent advantage was an artifact. With few iterations the cutoff interval is estimated from too little information, becomes narrower than its nominal width, and flags fitting items at an inflated rate. Detection was in effect bought with false positives. The false positive rates reported in the earlier paper were calculated per item, while the probability of at least one false flag across all items in a scale, the familywise error rate (FWER), was not examined. In addition, the guidance conditioned the number of iterations on sample size, while the convergence of the cutoff interval turns out to depend on the interval width alone.

Three contributions follow. First, the interval width and the number of iterations must be chosen jointly. The width sets the FWER of the interval decision rule, and the number of iterations determines whether the nominal width is attained at all. Second, the same bootstrap supports p-values with multiplicity corrections. The Westfall-Young step-down [@westfall_resampling_1993] targets the FWER directly and controls it when all items fit, detects more misfit than the interval rule at matched error rates, and needs far fewer iterations than the interval rule or the Holm procedure. The Benjamini-Hochberg procedure [@benjamini_controlling_1995], which controls the false discovery rate instead, is included for comparison and comes with an iteration floor that grows with the number of comparisons. Third, the paper introduces decision stability as an outcome in its own right: whether re-running the same analysis on the same data with a different random seed produces the same set of flagged items.

Results are presented using two simple performance metrics, detection rate and false positive rate, with decision stability added as a third. Readers interested in the statistical foundations of the multiple testing methods are referred to Westfall and Young [-@westfall_resampling_1993] and to the more recent paper by Ferreira [-@ferreiraMethodsTestingSmall2024]. All analyses use conditional item fit as implemented in the `iarm` R package [@mueller_iarm_2022], accessed through `easyRasch2` [@johanssonEasyRasch2PsychometricAnalysis2026]. The bootstrap is parametric throughout. Datasets are simulated from the Rasch model fitted to the observed data, and the model is refitted to every simulated dataset, so the item parameters are re-estimated in each bootstrap sample. The next section defines the procedure in full. The reasons to avoid unconditional item fit statistics, which is implemented in most other software, are detailed in Müller [-@muller_item_2020].

The paper proceeds as follows. The next section describes three properties of the bootstrap procedure that together motivate the simulation studies. The Method section describes the simulation design. Three results sections then cover interval convergence and error rates, the comparison between interval-based and p-value-based decisions, and decision stability. The Discussion summarizes the findings as practical recommendations.

# The interval, its width, and the number of iterations

The procedure under study uses a parametric bootstrap to establish critical values for conditional item infit [@muller_item_2020]. Item thresholds are estimated from the observed data by conditional maximum likelihood, and person locations by weighted likelihood [@warm_weighted_1989]. Each of $B$ simulated datasets then draws $n$ person locations with replacement from the estimated ones and generates responses under the Rasch model, or the partial credit model for polytomous items [@masters_rasch_1982], with the estimated thresholds. Every simulated dataset therefore fits the model by construction. The model is refitted to each simulated dataset by conditional maximum likelihood, so the item parameters are re-estimated in every bootstrap sample as they are in the analysis of the observed data, and conditional infit is computed from that refit. This yields an empirical null distribution of $B$ values per item, against which the observed infit of each item is compared. The procedure was evaluated in Johansson [-@johansson_detecting_2025] using the `easyRasch` package. Its successor `easyRasch2` [@johanssonEasyRasch2PsychometricAnalysis2026], which is used throughout this paper, summarizes each item's null distribution with a highest density interval of width $w$, and an observed infit value outside the interval flags the item as misfitting. This section describes three properties of that procedure which together motivate the simulation studies. Readers who prefer to see the consequences before the mechanics can skim the equations and return after the results sections.

## Draws per tail

The endpoints of the interval are extreme order statistics of the $B$ simulated values. The expected number of simulated values beyond the interval is $(1 - w)B$, or about $(1 - w)B/2$ in each tail. This quantity, draws per tail, governs how well the interval endpoints can be estimated at all. @tbl-drawspertail shows that common settings leave less than one simulated value per tail. As an example, $w = .999$ with $B = 250$, the defaults in `easyRasch2` 1.1.0, gives an expected count of 0.125. The interval then simply equals the range of the simulated values, the nominal width is not attained, and the realized width keeps growing as $B$ increases. A cutoff interval is therefore only defined once $B$ is large enough for the chosen $w$, and the required $B$ depends on $w$ alone. Sample size, which the iteration guidance in Johansson [-@johansson_detecting_2025] was conditioned on, plays no role in this convergence. One aim of this paper is to provide simulation-based grounds for choosing $w$ and $B$.

```{r tbl-drawspertail}
#| tbl-cap: "Draws per tail of the cutoff interval"
ws <- c(0.90, 0.95, 0.99, 0.995, 0.999)
bs <- c(100, 250, 400, 1000, 2000, 5000)
tab <- outer(ws, bs, function(w, B) (1 - w) / 2 * B)
dimnames(tab) <- list(paste0("w = ", ws), paste0("B = ", bs))
knitr::kable(tab, digits = 2)
```

*Note.* Expected number of simulated values per tail, $(1 - w)B/2$. Values below roughly 5 mean that the interval endpoints are poorly estimated and the realized interval is narrower than its nominal width.

## The width is the error rate of the interval rule

Once the interval has converged to its nominal width, a fitting item is flagged with probability $1 - w$. With $k$ items tested jointly, and treating the item statistics as independent, the probability that at least one fitting item is flagged is

$$
\text{FWER} = 1 - w^k,
$$ {#eq-fwer}

the FWER of the interval rule [@sidak_rectangular_1967]. The width is thus not a display choice but the error rate parameter of the decision procedure. For a 20-item scale, $w = .999$ gives a FWER of 2.0% while $w = .99$ gives 18.2%. Solving @eq-fwer for $w$ at $\text{FWER} = .05$ shows that the default $w = .999$ corresponds to a 51-item scale. Item fit statistics are positively dependent through the shared total score, which makes @eq-fwer a slightly conservative upper bound in practice. The simulation studies below confirm this across item counts and item formats.

## Bootstrap p-values and multiplicity corrections

The same $B$ simulated values support a different decision rule. Let $F_i$ denote the observed infit of item $i$ and $F^*_{ib}$ the simulated values. Each is studentized by the simulation mean and standard deviation, $t_i = (F_i - \bar{F}^*_i)/s^*_i$, which puts items with different locations on a common scale, since the expected infit range varies with item location relative to the sample [@muller_item_2020]. This follows Ferreira [-@ferreiraMethodsTestingSmall2024, Section 4], who standardizes each statistic by its mean and variance under the null so that the maximum across comparisons treats them on an equal footing. In his permutation setting those moments are known and are the same for the observed and the permuted statistics. Here they are estimated from the simulated values, a difference the next paragraphs return to. The marginal Monte Carlo p-value is

$$
p_i = \frac{1 + \sum_{b=1}^{B} I\left(|t^*_{ib}| \geq |t_i|\right)}{B + 1},
$$ {#eq-pmarg}

where $I(\cdot)$ equals 1 when its argument is true and 0 otherwise.

Its smallest attainable value is $1/(B+1)$, which sets the resolution of the test. When the observed statistic and the simulated ones are exchangeable under the null, as the observed and permuted statistics of a permutation test are, a p-value of this form is valid at any $B$ [@dufour_monte_2006, Proposition 2.2]. Two features of the procedure prevent that here, and the simulations measure the consequences of both.

First, the null hypothesis is composite. Item thresholds and person locations are estimated from the observed data, and the simulated datasets are drawn from the fitted model rather than from the model that generated the data. Dufour [-@dufour_monte_2006, Section 6] calls a test of this kind, with the nuisance parameters replaced by a point estimate, a local Monte Carlo test, and shows that it is valid asymptotically under regularity conditions rather than at a given sample size. The procedure therefore belongs to the bootstrap methods that Ferreira [-@ferreiraMethodsTestingSmall2024, Section 5] describes as controlling error rates approximately, with an accuracy at finite sample sizes that depends on the data and has to be checked rather than assumed. Validity at a given sample size would require removing the nuisance parameters, either by maximizing the Monte Carlo p-value over them [@dufour_monte_2006] or, for dichotomous items, by conditioning on the sufficient statistics and sampling response matrices with the observed margins [@verhelst_efficient_2008]. Neither is studied here. Second, the observed statistic is studentized by moments that it did not contribute to, while each simulated statistic is studentized by moments that include it. The observed statistic therefore varies slightly more about those moments than the simulated ones do, and the test is slightly liberal, by an amount that shrinks as $1/B$. Studentizing all $B + 1$ values by a mean and standard deviation computed over the observed and simulated values together removes this asymmetry, because the observed dataset is then treated as one of $B + 1$ datasets on equal terms. This joint studentization is the Monte Carlo counterpart of Ferreira's standardization by moments that the observed and resampled statistics share. The error-rate study evaluates both versions on the same simulated values.

Either way, the marginal p-value controls the error rate of a single pre-specified comparison. Scanning all $k$ items inflates the familywise error toward the levels in @eq-fwer, which is the argument for correcting it, not for abandoning p-values.

The Westfall-Young step-down corrects for multiplicity using the joint distribution that the bootstrap already provides [@westfall_resampling_1993; @ferreiraMethodsTestingSmall2024]. The most extreme observed statistic is compared against the distribution of the maximum across all items,

$$
\tilde{p}_{(1)} = \frac{1 + \sum_{b=1}^{B} I\left(\max_i |t^*_{ib}| \geq |t_{(1)}|\right)}{B + 1},
$$ {#eq-wy}

after which the maximum is recomputed over the remaining items for the next statistic, with monotonicity enforced. Only $B \geq 1/\alpha$ iterations, that is 20 at $\alpha = .05$, are needed for a rejection to be possible at all. Ferreira [-@ferreiraMethodsTestingSmall2024, Section 3] derives the step-down as a shortcut to the closure principle, which is valid under the subset pivotality condition of Westfall and Young [-@westfall_resampling_1993]: for every set of true hypotheses, the joint distribution of their statistics must be the same whether or not the remaining hypotheses are true. The bootstrap draws every simulated dataset from a model in which all items fit, so its reference distribution is that of the complete null by construction. Whether the observed statistics of fitting items follow it when other items misfit is a separate question. Ferreira's Example 2, a set of tests of pairwise correlations computed from the same variables, shows that the condition fails when the statistics share data in this way, and every conditional fit statistic shares the total score it is conditioned on. The step-down can therefore be expected to control the FWER when all items fit, which is weak control, but not necessarily when some items misfit.

The Benjamini-Hochberg procedure [@benjamini_controlling_1995] instead controls the false discovery rate, the expected proportion of flagged items that are in fact fitting. When a single item stands out, its adjusted p-value is bounded below by $m/(B+1)$ for $m$ comparisons, so it cannot be flagged unless

$$
B \geq \frac{m}{\alpha}.
$$ {#eq-bhfloor}

More generally, when $s$ comparisons have p-values at the Monte Carlo floor of @eq-pmarg, the smallest attainable adjusted p-value is $m/(s(B+1))$, so several clearly misfitting items lower the required $B$. Both floors follow from requiring the smallest attainable adjusted p-value to fall strictly below $\alpha$. With 20 items and $\alpha = .05$, a single misfitting item cannot be flagged unless $B \geq 400$.

The Holm procedure [@holm_simple_1979] is the familiar FWER alternative that uses the marginal p-values alone. It controls the FWER under general conditions, needs no pivotality condition, and among procedures based on the marginal p-values alone little improvement on it is possible [@ferreiraMethodsTestingSmall2024, Section 2]. Procedures that use the joint distribution of the statistics, such as the step-down above, can be more powerful when the statistics are dependent, but the gain is small when they are close to independent, and the agreement with @eq-fwer reported below suggests that item fit statistics are close to independent. With Monte Carlo p-values Holm also has a reachability floor. Its smallest adjusted p-value is $m/(B+1)$ for $m$ comparisons, the floor of @eq-bhfloor, and unlike that of Benjamini-Hochberg it is not lowered when several items stand out. Ferreira [-@ferreiraMethodsTestingSmall2024] gives a self-contained account of these methods aimed at the range of 5 to 50 hypotheses, which corresponds to the range encountered in item-level analysis.

In summary, several decision rules can be computed from one bootstrap. The interval rule has its error rate set by $w$ and needs a large $B$ for extreme widths. The Westfall-Young p-value targets the FWER directly and can reject from 20 iterations. The Holm and Benjamini-Hochberg p-values control the FWER and the false discovery rate from the marginal p-values, and both have a reachability floor that grows with the number of comparisons. All of them inherit the approximate validity of the bootstrap they are computed from, and the simulation studies quantify how close each comes to its nominal error rate.

# Method

```{r method-prep}
#| include: false
real_fit <- s_cal$real_fit
rf <- setNames(sprintf("%.2f", real_fit$Infit_MSQ), real_fit$Item)
anch <- aggregate(infit ~ rho, data = s_cal$anchor, FUN = mean)
anch <- anch[order(anch$rho), ]
av <- sprintf("%.2f", anch$infit)   # rho .75, .85, .90
# five-item calibration (calibration_rho_short.R), pooled over n
m5 <- function(r) mean(s_cal5$grid$infit[abs(s_cal5$grid$rho - r) < 1e-9], na.rm = TRUE)
# twenty-item polytomous scan and the nine-item phq9 anchor, both at the same rho
p20 <- function(r) mean(s_cal$grid$infit[abs(s_cal$grid$rho - r) < 1e-9 &
                                         s_cal$grid$format == "polytomous"], na.rm = TRUE)
ph85 <- function() mean(s_cal$anchor$infit[abs(s_cal$anchor$rho - 0.85) < 1e-9], na.rm = TRUE)
# descriptives of the phq9 data behind the real item set
ph_obs <- load_phq9_arm()$obs
ph_tot <- rowSums(ph_obs)
ph_zero <- sprintf("%.1f", 100 * mean(ph_tot == 0))
ph_med <- sprintf("%.0f", median(ph_tot))
ph_max <- 3 * ncol(ph_obs)
ph_z <- function(it) sprintf("%.0f", 100 * mean(ph_obs[, it] == 0))
```

## Overview

Seven simulation studies were conducted, and @tbl-studies summarizes their designs. Each answers one question, and its design follows from that question.

The first two use the 20 dichotomous items of Johansson [-@johansson_detecting_2025], so that the iteration guidance of that paper is re-examined on the item set it was derived from. The first asks how many iterations the cutoff interval needs at a given width. Convergence concerns the null distribution alone, so the study uses null data only, and it runs to $B$ = 10 000 to provide a reference width. The second asks what error rates the decision rules have across a grid of widths and iteration counts, which needs null conditions for the familywise error and misfit conditions for detection. Its misfit uses $\rho$ = .15, the strong misfit of the earlier paper, so that its detection results connect to that paper.

The third moves to polytomous items with misfit severity anchored on the infit values of a real dataset, as described below, so that the decision rules are compared at a severity that analysts observe rather than at one chosen to be detectable. It uses two item sets, PHQ-9 item parameters for a real configuration and a stylised 15-item set for a regular one. The fourth holds datasets fixed and varies only the bootstrap seed, because decision stability concerns one dataset analyzed twice, which variation between datasets would obscure. It spans misfit from strong ($\rho$ = .15) to anchored ($\rho$ = .85), since stability depends on how many items lie near the decision threshold and that number varies with misfit severity. The fifth replaces multidimensionality with random responding at matched infit, to check whether two findings belong to the misfit mechanism rather than to misfit in general, and is reported alongside the rule comparisons it checks. The sixth asks whether the decision rules transfer to conditional outfit, the second fit statistic the same bootstrap already produces. It holds the rule and the number of iterations fixed at the recommended settings and varies only the statistic. The seventh repeats the error-rate and rule comparisons on a five-item scale, below the range the other studies cover, where @eq-fwer predicts the lowest error rates and the reachability floor of Benjamini-Hochberg no longer binds. Replication counts differ because the studies estimate different quantities with different precision, and the Monte Carlo error of each is reported in @tbl-mcse.

In the first five studies, all five interval widths ($w$ = .90, .95, .99, .995, and .999) are evaluated from the same simulated values. The first measures the interval itself and computes no decision rules; in the second to the fifth, all four rules are computed from the same bootstrap within each replication, so comparisons between rules are paired. In the two dichotomous studies each replication also runs a single bootstrap at the largest number of iterations, and every smaller $B$ is evaluated on its first $B$ draws, so comparisons between values of $B$ are paired within the bootstrap as well. The two studies share their null replications, from which the first reads the interval and the second the decision rules. The sixth study holds the rule fixed at the Westfall-Young p-value with $B$ = 1000 and varies the fit statistic instead. Both statistics are again read from the same bootstrap, so that comparison is paired in the same sense. The seventh returns to the full set of widths and rules.

| Study | Items | $\rho$ | Misfitting items | $n$ | $B$ | Replications |
|:-------------------|:-------------------|:------------|:-----------|:----------|:------------|:--------------|
| Interval convergence | 20 dichotomous | none | 0 | 150 to 1000 | 100 to 10 000 | 500 |
| Error rates over $(w, B)$ | 20 dichotomous | .15 | 0, 1, 3 | 150 to 1000 | 100 to 10 000 | 500 / 250 |
| PHQ-9-anchored misfit | 15 polytomous, 9 phq9 | .75, .85, .90 | 0 to 3 | 150 to 1000 | 100, 400, 2000 | 120 |
| Decision stability | 15 polytomous, 9 phq9 | .15, .50, .85 | 0 or all | 250, 1000 | 100 to 2000 | 10 datasets x 25 seeds |
| Mechanism check | 9 phq9 | random responses | 1, 2 | 250, 1000 | 100, 400, 2000 | 120 |
| Infit versus outfit | 20 dichotomous, 9 phq9 | .60, .85 | 0, 1 | 250, 600 | 1000 | 250 |
| Short scale | 5 polytomous | .75 | 0, 1 | 250, 600 | 100, 400, 2000 | 1000 / 250 |

: Overview of the simulation studies {#tbl-studies}

*Note.* Misfitting item counts are 1 and 3 for the 20-item and 15-item sets and 1 and 2 for the 9-item set, with 0 denoting the null condition used for error rates. The $n$ = 150 condition is included for the 9-item set only. In the sixth study the two correlations belong to the two item sets in the order listed, chosen so that both inject comparable infit, and its single misfitting item is run as two separate conditions, once near the person mean and once off target. The first two studies share their null replications, 500 per sample size, which run to $B$ = 10 000. The misfit conditions of the second study run to $B$ = 2000 with 250 replications each. The seventh study uses 1000 replications for its null conditions, which carry the error-rate claim, and 250 for its misfit conditions.

## Data generation

Misfit is induced by multidimensionality, as in Johansson [-@johansson_detecting_2025], in every study but the mechanism check. Fitting items are generated from a primary latent dimension and misfitting items from a second dimension, with person locations drawn from a bivariate normal distribution where $\rho$ denotes the correlation between the two dimensions. Lower values of $\rho$ produce stronger misfit. The null conditions, with no misfitting items, use a single dimension.

The mechanism check replaces multidimensionality with random responding, in which a fixed proportion of the responses to the target items is replaced by a uniform draw over the response categories. That proportion was set so that a single target item has the same expected infit as in the multidimensional condition, which puts the two mechanisms on equal footing at matched misfit severity.

The dichotomous item set replicates the design of the earlier paper: 20 items with locations drawn uniformly between -2 and 2 logits, person locations with a standard deviation of 1.5, and response data generated with the `eRm` package [@mair_extended_2007]. Misfitting items are those located nearest 0, -1, and -2 logits relative to the person mean, so that targeting varies. Johansson [-@johansson_detecting_2025] drew every sample from one master dataset of 10 000 simulated respondents per condition. Here every replication of every study generates its respondents anew, so replications are independent and no chance feature of one master dataset is shared by all the replications of a condition. The sixth study reuses this item set and contrasts two single-item conditions, one misfitting the item nearest the person mean at 0.04 logits and one misfitting the most off-target item at 1.82 logits. This mirrors the q5 and q8 contrast in the PHQ-9 set (see below).

The polytomous item sets use four ordered response categories. The stylised set has 15 items with locations evenly spaced between -2 and 2 logits and item thresholds spread one logit around each location, again with person standard deviation 1.5. The second set takes its item parameters from the phq9 dataset included in `easyRasch2`, nine depression screening items with four response categories answered by 600 respondents. The data are a subsample of the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey [@cdc_nhanes_2024] in which respondents with all-zero responses were randomly thinned, to avoid the zero-inflated response pattern of the full survey data. In the resulting data `r ph_zero`% of respondents have a total score of 0 and the median total score is `r ph_med` of `r ph_max`, so the sample leans toward the upper half of the scale. Zero responses are concentrated in two items, q8 (`r ph_z(8)`%) and q9 (`r ph_z(9)`%), the items located furthest above the person mean. The configuration is therefore unusual in having two off-target items rather than in having a floor effect, and the stylised 15-item set provides a regular configuration for comparison. Thresholds were estimated with conditional maximum likelihood and the latent standard deviation of 1.39 was estimated from the same data. This set represents the item properties of a real instrument rather than stylised ones. Its misfitting items were designated to be q5, located near the person mean, and q8, the most off-target item at 1.4 logits above the mean, so that targeting again varies.

## Calibrating misfit severity

Misfit severity is reported and calibrated on the infit scale rather than on $\rho$, for two reasons. First, the same $\rho$ produces very different infit depending on item format. @tbl-calibration shows that at identical item locations and person distributions, polytomous items yield roughly 2.8 times the infit excess of dichotomous items, because more response categories carry more information per item. The $\rho$ = .15 used in the earlier paper was chosen to represent a clearly misfitting dichotomous item. Carried unchanged into polytomous items it would produce infit values beyond what real data show. Second, infit is the scale on which analysts observe misfit, so calibrating on it connects the simulation conditions to practice.

The same non-portability holds across item counts. A separate scan on the five-item set used in the short-scale study gives a mean injected infit of `r sprintf("%.2f", m5(0.85))` at $\rho$ = .85, against `r sprintf('%.2f', p20(0.85))` for the same $\rho$ on the twenty-item polytomous set built to the same recipe, with the nine phq9 items falling between at `r sprintf('%.2f', ph85())`. Reaching the anchored range at five items requires $\rho$ = .75, which gives `r sprintf("%.2f", m5(0.75))`. A short scale needs stronger misfit to show the same infit, because the misfitting item is a larger share of the total score that the statistic is conditioned on and therefore attenuates its own value more. Anchoring on infit rather than on $\rho$ keeps the conditions comparable across item counts as well as formats.  We remind readers that infit is strongly dependent on sample size [@muller_item_2020] and traditional rule-of-thumb thresholds should be avoided when interpreting infit values.

```{r tbl-calibration}
#| tbl-cap: "Conditional infit by item format and inter-dimensional correlation"
cal <- s_cal$grid |>
  summarise(infit = mean(infit, na.rm = TRUE), .by = c(rho, format)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = format, values_from = infit) |>
  arrange(rho) |>
  mutate(ratio = (polytomous - 1) / (dichotomous - 1))
knitr::kable(cal, digits = 2,
             col.names = c("Correlation", "Dichotomous", "Polytomous",
                           "Excess ratio"))
```

*Note.* Mean conditional infit of a single misfitting item under identical conditions (20 items, identical locations, $n$ = 500, 60 replications). The excess ratio is the polytomous infit excess over 1.0 divided by the dichotomous excess.

The misfit level used for the rule comparisons, referred to below as the PHQ-9-anchored or anchored level, is set against the phq9 dataset with $n$ = 600. Analyzing the observed responses with simulation-based cutoffs ($B$ = 1000) and Westfall-Young corrected p-values flags three underfitting items, q3 at `r rf["q3"]`, q8 at `r rf["q8"]`, and q9 at `r rf["q9"]`, along with two overfitting items at `r rf["q2"]` and `r rf["q4"]`. A calibration scan on the phq9 item parameters shows that $\rho$ = .85 and .90 together reproduce this range, with mean infit values of `r av[2]` and `r av[3]` for a single misfitting item, close to the strongest and the mildest flagged real items. The level .75 gives `r av[1]`, slightly beyond the worst real item. The stability study additionally includes $\rho$ = .15 and .50 to span the range from the strong misfit used in the earlier paper down to the anchored level.

Matching mean conditional infit places a misfitting item at the same observed severity on the statistic that analysts see, which is why it was chosen. It does not equate the alternative distributions, the contamination of the conditioning score or the difficulty of detection, and the mechanism check reported below shows that conditions with the same mean infit can produce very different false positive rates. The anchored level is therefore one empirically observed severity, under multidimensionality, and not a representative sample of the misfit that analysts encounter.

## Decision rules and performance metrics

Four decision rules are compared, each computed from the same bootstrap as the others wherever more than one is evaluated. The interval rule flags an item when its observed infit falls outside the highest density interval, evaluated at each of the five widths. The three p-value rules flag an item when its marginal, Westfall-Young corrected, or Benjamini-Hochberg corrected p-value falls below $\alpha$ = .05, as described in the previous section.

Three performance metrics are reported. The detection rate is the percentage of misfitting items that are flagged. The false positive rate is the percentage of fitting items that are flagged. The familywise false positive rate is the percentage of replications in which at least one fitting item is flagged, which under the null conditions estimates the familywise error rate that @eq-fwer describes. The stability metrics are defined in their own section below.

## Software and execution

All simulations were run in R 4.6.1 using `easyRasch2` [@johanssonEasyRasch2PsychometricAnalysis2026], which computes conditional item fit through the `iarm` package [@mueller_iarm_2022] and estimates item parameters with conditional maximum likelihood. Results were produced under `easyRasch2` versions 1.1.0 and 1.1.1, and the two dichotomous studies under version 1.4.0. The versions are identical in everything the simulations use, apart from the `statistic` argument added in 1.1.1 that the infit-versus-outfit study requires. As a check, a cell of the original dichotomous study rebuilt under 1.4.0 reproduced its p-values and interval flags to the last digit. In the polytomous studies every combination of replication and iteration count uses an independent bootstrap. In the two dichotomous studies the values of $B$ are nested within one bootstrap per replication, as described above. Seeds are deterministic functions of the design cell, so any cell can be reproduced in isolation. Simulation code and cached results are available in the repository accompanying this paper, as described in the Reproducibility section.

# Interval convergence and error rates

```{r r4-prep}
#| include: false
# --- convergence study -------------------------------------------------------
CV <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(s_conv$grid)), function(i) {
  r <- s_conv$res[[i]]
  if (is.null(r)) return(NULL)
  cbind(rep = s_conv$grid$rep[i], n = s_conv$grid$n[i], r)
}))
relw <- CV |>
  summarise(v = median(width), .by = c(n, w, B)) |>
  mutate(rel = v / v[B == max(B)], .by = c(n, w))

# largest discrepancy between sample sizes, over all (w, B)
n_spread <- relw |>
  summarise(sp = max(rel) - min(rel), .by = c(w, B)) |>
  summarise(mx = max(sp)) |> pull(mx)

# smallest B reaching 99 percent of the converged width
b99 <- relw |>
  summarise(m = median(rel), .by = c(w, B)) |>
  summarise(B99 = min(B[m >= 0.99]), .by = w) |> arrange(w)
bq <- function(wv) format(b99$B99[abs(b99$w - wv) < 1e-9], big.mark = " ")

rwn <- function(wv, Bv) median(
  relw$rel[abs(relw$w - wv) < 1e-9 & relw$B == Bv])
rw <- function(wv, Bv) sprintf("%.2f", rwn(wv, Bv))
# percent by which the interval falls short of its converged width
short <- function(wv, Bv, dp = 0) sprintf(paste0("%.", dp, "f"),
                                          100 * (1 - rwn(wv, Bv)))

# --- five-item short scale: BH vs WY, paired within replication --------------
P7 <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(s_short$grid)), function(i) {
  r <- s_short$res[[i]]$pval
  if (is.null(r)) return(NULL)
  g <- s_short$grid[i, c("k", "n", "rep"), drop = FALSE]
  rownames(g) <- NULL
  cbind(g, r)
})) |>
  mutate(is_mis = k > 0 & item == s_short$mis)
rules5 <- P7 |>
  filter(k > 0, B == 2000) |>
  summarise(det_wy = 100 * mean(padj_fwer[is_mis] < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE),
            det_bh = 100 * mean(padj_bh[is_mis] < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE),
            fp_wy  = 100 * mean(padj_fwer[!is_mis] < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE),
            fp_bh  = 100 * mean(padj_bh[!is_mis] < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE),
            .by = n)
# named bh5 to avoid clashing with the r5 data frame in the section 5 prep chunk
bh5 <- function(nn, f) sprintf("%.1f", rules5[[f]][rules5$n == nn])

# --- five-item short scale (study 7): familywise rates under the null ---------
S7 <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(s_short$grid)), function(i) {
  r <- s_short$res[[i]]$hdci
  if (is.null(r)) return(NULL)
  g <- s_short$grid[i, c("k", "n", "rep"), drop = FALSE]
  rownames(g) <- NULL
  cbind(g, r)
}))
fwe5 <- S7 |>
  filter(k == 0, B == 2000) |>
  summarise(any = as.integer(sum(code > 0) > 0), .by = c(w, n, rep)) |>
  summarise(pct = 100 * mean(any), R = n(), .by = c(w, n)) |>
  mutate(pred = 100 * (1 - w^5),
         se = 100 * sqrt((pct / 100) * (1 - pct / 100) / R),
         z = (pct - pred) / se) |>
  arrange(n, w)
maxz5 <- max(abs(fwe5$z))
reps5 <- max(fwe5$R)
# bootstraps that produced no usable p-value at all
drop5 <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(s_short$grid)), function(i) {
  r <- s_short$res[[i]]$pval
  if (is.null(r)) return(NULL)
  g <- s_short$grid[i, c("k", "n", "rep"), drop = FALSE]
  rownames(g) <- NULL
  cbind(g, r)
})) |>
  summarise(bad = all(is.na(p_marg)), .by = c(k, n, B, rep)) |>
  filter(n == 250) |>
  summarise(n_bad = sum(bad), n_all = n()) 
# the five widths in ascending order, as a readable inline list
s5 <- function(nn) {
  v <- fwe5$pct[fwe5$n == nn][order(fwe5$w[fwe5$n == nn])]
  paste0(paste(sprintf("%.1f", v[-length(v)]), collapse = ", "),
         " and ", sprintf("%.1f", v[length(v)]), " percent")
}

# --- familywise error under the null, all three item sets --------------------
G0 <- bind_part(s_grid, "hdci", c("rep", "k", "n")) |>
  filter(k == 0) |> mutate(items = 20L, arm = "20 dichotomous")
P0 <- bind_part(s_poly, "hdci", c("arm", "rep", "k", "n", "rho")) |>
  filter(k == 0) |>
  mutate(items = ifelse(arm == "sim15", 15L, 9L),
         arm = ifelse(arm == "sim15", "15 polytomous", "9 phq9"))
NUL <- bind_rows(G0 |> select(arm, items, rep, n, B, w, item, code),
                 P0 |> select(arm, items, rep, n, B, w, item, code))
fwe <- NUL |>
  summarise(any = any(code > 0), .by = c(arm, items, w, B, n, rep)) |>
  summarise(obs = 100 * mean(any), .by = c(arm, items, w, B)) |>
  mutate(pred = 100 * (1 - w^items))
fq <- function(arm_, wv, Bv) sprintf("%.1f", fwe$obs[
  fwe$arm == arm_ & abs(fwe$w - wv) < 1e-9 & fwe$B == Bv])
pq <- function(arm_, wv) sprintf("%.1f", unique(fwe$pred[
  fwe$arm == arm_ & abs(fwe$w - wv) < 1e-9]))

# agreement with the Sidak prediction for the widths converged at B = 2000
conv_ok <- fwe |> filter(B == 2000, w <= 0.99) |> mutate(ratio = obs / pred)

# --- the artifact: detection and false positives at w = .999 -----------------
ART <- bind_part(s_grid, "hdci", c("rep", "k", "n")) |>
  filter(k == 3, abs(w - 0.999) < 1e-9) |>
  mutate(is_mis = item %in% s_grid$misfit) |>
  summarise(det = 100 * mean(code[is_mis] > 0),
            fp = 100 * mean(code[!is_mis] > 0), .by = c(n, B)) |>
  arrange(n, B)
aq <- function(n_, col, dp = 0) paste(sprintf(paste0("%.", dp, "f"),
                                              ART[[col]][ART$n == n_]),
                                      collapse = ", ")
fw999 <- fwe |> filter(arm == "20 dichotomous", abs(w - 0.999) < 1e-9)

# single misfitting item, same item set: detection is at ceiling throughout
k1det <- bind_part(s_grid, "hdci", c("rep", "k", "n")) |>
  filter(k == 1, abs(w - 0.999) < 1e-9, n == 150,
         item == s_grid$misfit[1]) |>
  summarise(det = 100 * mean(code > 0), .by = B)
```

This section reports the two studies that use dichotomous items, together with the null conditions of the polytomous studies. The first question is how many iterations the cutoff interval needs before it attains its nominal width. The second is what the error rate of the interval rule then is, and whether @eq-fwer describes it.

## How many iterations the interval needs

@fig-convergence shows the median interval width at each number of iterations, expressed relative to the width obtained from all 10 000 iterations of the same bootstrap, the reference width. Two results follow. First, the required number of iterations depends on the width and not on the sample size. Lines for the same width overlap almost exactly across the four sample sizes, with a largest discrepancy of `r sprintf("%.3f", n_spread)` at any combination of width and iterations. Convergence is a property of the simulated null distribution and its tails, and the sample size affects where that distribution sits rather than how many values are needed to describe its extremes.

```{r fig-convergence}
#| fig-cap: "Convergence of the cutoff interval"
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4
relw |>
  mutate(w = factor(sprintf("%.3f", w)), n = factor(n)) |>
  ggplot(aes(B, rel, colour = w, linetype = w, shape = w,
             group = interaction(w, n))) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linewidth = 0.4, colour = "grey70") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_point(size = 1.6) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(100, 400, 1000, 2000, 5000, 10000),
                labels = c("100", "400", "1000", "2000", "5000", "10 000")) +
  scale_bw("Interval width", colours = pal_ramp5) +
  labs(x = "Bootstrap iterations (B), log scale",
       y = "Width relative to B = 10 000") +
  theme_paper(11)
```

*Note.* Median cutoff interval width at each number of iterations, relative to the width at 10 000 iterations of the same bootstrap, for four sample sizes and five interval widths. Each line is one combination of width and sample size, with the width shown by line type and point shape. Lines of the same width overlap, showing that convergence does not depend on sample size. Values below 1 indicate an interval narrower than its nominal width.

Second, the number of iterations required grows sharply as the interval widens. Taking 99% of that reference width as a criterion, `r bq(0.95)` iterations suffice for $w$ = .95, `r bq(0.99)` for $w$ = .99, and `r bq(0.999)` for $w$ = .999. The reference is empirical rather than asymptotic: at $w$ = .999 it has only five draws per tail itself, so the shortfall reported for that width is if anything understated. At 100 iterations the .999 interval reaches only `r rw(0.999, 100)` of that reference, that is roughly a quarter too narrow, while the .95 interval is already within `r short(0.95, 100)` percent. This is the pattern that @tbl-drawspertail predicts. Widths near 1 place their endpoints far into the tails of the simulated distribution, where few or no simulated values fall, so the interval collapses toward the range of the simulation.

## Error rates of the interval rule

@fig-fwe shows the familywise false positive rate under the null conditions, for all three item sets, against the prediction of @eq-fwer. At iteration counts where the interval has converged, the prediction describes the observed rates well. For the widths .90 to .99 at 2000 iterations, the ratio of observed to predicted rates ranges from `r sprintf("%.2f", min(conv_ok$ratio))` to `r sprintf("%.2f", max(conv_ok$ratio))` across all three item sets, with most values slightly below 1. The mild conservatism is expected, since item fit statistics are positively dependent through the shared total score and @eq-fwer assumes independence. The interval width therefore sets the familywise error rate of the decision rule, and it does so consistently across 9, 15, and 20 items and across dichotomous and polytomous formats.

The relation also holds below that range, where it is most exposed. On a five-item polytomous scale @eq-fwer predicts markedly lower rates of 41.0, 22.6, 4.9, 2.5 and 0.5 percent for the five widths, so a bound that was loose because of dependence among item statistics would show it here. From `r format(reps5, big.mark = " ")` null replications per condition at $B$ = 2000, the observed rates were `r s5(600)` at $n$ = 600 and `r s5(250)` at $n$ = 250. No width departs from its prediction by more than `r sprintf("%.1f", maxz5)` Monte Carlo standard errors at either sample size, and at $n$ = 600 the two widest intervals fall below their predictions, the same mild conservatism seen at 9, 15, and 20 items. Equation 1 therefore describes five-item scales as well as longer ones.

```{r fig-fwe}
#| fig-cap: "Familywise false positive rate against the prediction of @eq-fwer"
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4
fwe |>
  mutate(arm = factor(arm, levels = c("9 phq9", "15 polytomous",
                                      "20 dichotomous"),
                      labels = c("9 phq9 items", "15 polytomous items",
                                      "20 dichotomous items"))) |>
  mutate(w = factor(sprintf("%.3f", w))) |>
  ggplot(aes(factor(B), obs, colour = w, linetype = w, shape = w, group = w)) +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = pred), colour = "grey65",
             linetype = "dotted", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_point(size = 1.6) +
  facet_wrap(~arm, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_x_discrete(guide = guide_axis(angle = 45)) +
  scale_bw("Interval width", colours = pal_ramp5) +
  labs(x = "Bootstrap iterations (B)",
       y = "Familywise false positives (%)") +
  theme_paper(12) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0,100))
```

*Note.* Rates under the null conditions, by interval width and number of iterations, for the three item sets. Dotted grey horizontal lines are the predictions of @eq-fwer, one for each width. Observed rates approach the prediction as the interval converges, and exceed it when too few iterations leave the interval narrower than its nominal width.

Where the interval has not converged, the observed rates lie above the prediction, and by a wide margin at the narrowest widths. For the 20 dichotomous items at $w$ = .999, whose nominal familywise error rate is `r pq("20 dichotomous", 0.999)`%, the observed rate was `r fq("20 dichotomous", 0.999, 100)`% at 100 iterations and `r fq("20 dichotomous", 0.999, 400)`% at 400. Even at 2000 iterations it remained `r fq("20 dichotomous", 0.999, 2000)`%, which is consistent with the interval still being `r short(0.999, 2000, 1)` percent narrower than the reference at that point. The two studies thus tell one story from two directions. A small shortfall in interval width translates into a large excess in familywise error, because the error rate is governed by the extreme tails that the shortfall affects.

## The detection and false positive trade-off across iterations

The recommendation of 100 to 400 iterations in Johansson [-@johansson_detecting_2025] rested on the observation that detection rates were highest with the fewest iterations. The present results show the same trade-off and explain its source. With three misfitting items among 20 dichotomous items at $n$ = 150, detection across 100, 200, 400, 1000, and 2000 iterations was `r aq(150, "det")`%, a decline of the same magnitude as the one reported in the earlier paper. The false positive rate on the fitting items in the same conditions was `r aq(150, "fp", 1)`%, and the familywise false positive rate under the null fell from `r fq("20 dichotomous", 0.999, 100)`% to `r fq("20 dichotomous", 0.999, 2000)`% over the same range. The decline in detection appears only where detection is not already at ceiling. With a single misfitting item in the same item set, detection stayed at or above `r sprintf("%.1f", min(k1det$det))`% at every number of iterations, and only the false positive rate responded.

Detection and false positives therefore decline together, and for the same reason. Fewer iterations produce a narrower interval, a narrower interval flags more items, and among the flagged items are both misfitting and fitting ones. The apparent advantage of few iterations was not greater sensitivity but a lower and undocumented threshold. Since the earlier paper evaluated false positives per item rather than across the scale, the cost was easy to overlook. A per-item rate of `r sprintf("%.0f", ART$fp[ART$n == 150 & ART$B == 100])`% at 100 iterations is unremarkable in isolation, while the corresponding probability of at least one false flag somewhere in a 20-item scale was `r fq("20 dichotomous", 0.999, 100)`%.

# Interval-based versus p-value-based decisions

```{r r5-prep}
#| include: false
al5 <- 0.05
GP <- bind_part(s_grid, "pval", c("rep", "k", "n"))

# null familywise error by rule and B, pooled over n (dichotomous, 20 items).
# Holm from the marginal p-values within each analysis. wyj = Westfall-Young
# with the observed and simulated statistics studentized jointly over all
# B + 1 values (computed in rev1/fresh_rerun.R from the same draws).
G0p <- GP |>
  filter(k == 0) |>
  mutate(p_holm = p.adjust(p_marg, "holm"), .by = c(rep, n, B))
null_any <- G0p |>
  mutate(unc = p_marg < al5, holm = p_holm < al5, wy = padj_fwer < al5,
         wyj = padj_fwer_pool < al5, bh = padj_bh < al5) |>
  summarise(across(c(unc, holm, wy, wyj, bh), any), .by = c(rep, n, B))
null_rules <- null_any |>
  summarise(across(c(unc, holm, wy, wyj, bh), ~100 * mean(.x)), .by = B) |>
  arrange(B)

# paired standard-minus-joint Westfall-Young difference per B
wyj_pair <- null_any |>
  mutate(d = as.numeric(wy) - as.numeric(wyj)) |>
  summarise(diff = 100 * mean(d), se = 100 * sd(d) / sqrt(n()), .by = B) |>
  arrange(B)
wjd <- function(B_, col = "diff") sprintf("%.1f", wyj_pair[[col]][wyj_pair$B == B_])
wjd_max_from <- function(from) sprintf("%.1f",
  max(abs(wyj_pair$diff[wyj_pair$B >= from])))

# per-item rejection rate of the marginal test under the null, against the
# largest size a valid Monte Carlo test can attain at that B
item_rate <- G0p |>
  summarise(rate = 100 * mean(p_marg < al5), .by = B) |>
  mutate(attain = 100 * floor(al5 * (B + 1) - 1e-9) / (B + 1))
ir_rng <- sprintf("%.1f to %.1f", min(item_rate$rate), max(item_rate$rate))

# Westfall-Young null rate in the polytomous studies, pooled, from B = 400
poly_wy0 <- bind_part(s_poly, "pval", c("arm", "rep", "k", "n", "rho")) |>
  filter(k == 0) |>
  summarise(any = any(padj_fwer < al5, na.rm = TRUE), .by = c(arm, rep, n, B)) |>
  summarise(pct = 100 * mean(any), .by = B)
pw_rng <- with(poly_wy0[poly_wy0$B >= 400, ],
               sprintf("%.1f and %.1f", min(pct), max(pct)))
nr <- function(col, B_) sprintf("%.1f", null_rules[[col]][null_rules$B == B_])
nr_rng <- function(col, from) {
  v <- null_rules[[col]][null_rules$B >= from]
  sprintf("%.1f and %.1f", min(v), max(v))
}
n_null <- GP |> filter(k == 0) |> distinct(rep, n, B) |> count(B) |> pull(n) |> unique()
stopifnot(length(n_null) == 1)

# BH, Holm and WY detection by B for k = 1 and k = 3 at n = 150. Holm is
# adjusted over all 20 items of each analysis before keeping the misfitting ones.
seqs <- GP |>
  filter(k > 0, n == 150) |>
  mutate(is_mis = mapply(function(k, it) it %in% s_grid$misfit[seq_len(k)],
                         k, item)) |>
  mutate(p_holm = p.adjust(p_marg, "holm"), .by = c(rep, k, n, B)) |>
  filter(is_mis) |>
  summarise(bh = 100 * mean(padj_bh < al5, na.rm = TRUE),
            holm = 100 * mean(p_holm < al5, na.rm = TRUE),
            wy = 100 * mean(padj_fwer < al5, na.rm = TRUE), .by = c(k, B)) |>
  arrange(k, B)
sq <- function(k_, rule_) paste(sprintf("%.0f", seqs[[rule_]][seqs$k == k_]),
                                collapse = ", ")

# anchored misfit level: all rules, both arms, rho = .85
RH <- bind_part(s_poly, "hdci", c("arm", "rep", "k", "n", "rho")) |>
  filter(abs(rho - 0.85) < 1e-9, k > 0)
RP <- bind_part(s_poly, "pval", c("arm", "rep", "k", "n", "rho")) |>
  filter(abs(rho - 0.85) < 1e-9, k > 0)
mis5 <- function(a, k) s_poly$arms[[a]]$mis[seq_len(k)]

r5_all <- bind_rows(
  RH |> filter(abs(w - 0.999) < 1e-9) |>
    transmute(arm, rep, k, n, B, item, flag = as.integer(code > 0),
              rule = "Interval, w = .999"),
  RP |> transmute(arm, rep, k, n, B, item, flag = as.integer(p_marg < al5),
                  rule = "Marginal p"),
  RP |> transmute(arm, rep, k, n, B, item,
                  flag = as.integer(padj_fwer < al5), rule = "Westfall-Young"),
  RP |> transmute(arm, rep, k, n, B, item,
                  flag = as.integer(padj_bh < al5), rule = "Benjamini-Hochberg"),
  # Holm from the marginal p-values, adjusted over all items of each analysis
  RP |> mutate(p_holm = p.adjust(p_marg, "holm"), .by = c(arm, rep, k, n, B)) |>
    transmute(arm, rep, k, n, B, item, flag = as.integer(p_holm < al5),
              rule = "Holm")
) |>
  mutate(is_mis = mapply(function(a, k, it) it %in% mis5(a, k), arm, k, item),
         cond = factor(paste0(arm, ", n = ", n),
                       levels = c("phq9, n = 150", "phq9, n = 250",
                                  "phq9, n = 1000", "sim15, n = 250",
                                  "sim15, n = 1000")))
# Figure 3 shows the four rules of the submission. Holm is reported in the text
# and in the appendix table of decision rules.
r5 <- r5_all |> filter(rule != "Holm")

# pooled false positives at B = 2000 by rule
fp2000 <- r5 |>
  filter(B == 2000, !is_mis) |>
  summarise(fp = 100 * mean(flag, na.rm = TRUE), .by = rule)
fpv <- function(rule_) sprintf("%.1f", fp2000$fp[fp2000$rule == rule_])
fp2000_h <- r5_all |>
  filter(B == 2000, !is_mis, rule == "Holm") |>
  summarise(fp = 100 * mean(flag, na.rm = TRUE)) |> pull(fp)

# Holm against Westfall-Young at the anchored level: detection at B = 100,
# and the paired detection difference at B = 2000
holm100 <- r5_all |>
  filter(B == 100, is_mis, rule == "Holm") |>
  summarise(det = 100 * mean(flag)) |> pull(det)
holm_gain <- r5_all |>
  filter(B == 2000, is_mis, rule %in% c("Holm", "Westfall-Young")) |>
  summarise(d = mean(flag), .by = c(arm, k, n, rep, rule)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = rule, values_from = d) |>
  mutate(diff = 100 * (`Westfall-Young` - Holm)) |>
  summarise(gain = mean(diff), se = sd(diff) / sqrt(n()), .by = c(arm, k, n))
hg_rng <- sprintf("%.1f and %.1f", min(holm_gain$gain), max(holm_gain$gain))
hg_se <- sprintf("%.1f", max(holm_gain$se))

# detection gain of WY over the interval at w = .999 and the matched w = .995,
# phq9 arm, B = 2000, paired within replications
gain_vs <- function(wv) {
  M <- inner_join(
    RH |> filter(abs(w - wv) < 1e-9, arm == "phq9", B == 2000) |>
      mutate(h = as.integer(code > 0)) |> select(rep, k, n, item, h),
    RP |> filter(arm == "phq9", B == 2000) |>
      mutate(f = as.integer(padj_fwer < al5)) |> select(rep, k, n, item, f),
    by = c("rep", "k", "n", "item")) |>
    mutate(is_mis = mapply(function(k, it) it %in% mis5("phq9", k), k, item))
  M |> filter(is_mis) |>
    summarise(g = 100 * (mean(f) - mean(h)), .by = c(k, n))
}
g999 <- gain_vs(0.999); g995 <- gain_vs(0.995)
rng <- function(g) sprintf("%.1f to %.1f", min(g$g[g$g > 1]), max(g$g))

# matched-width null check: observed familywise error of w = .995 for 9 items
H0 <- bind_part(s_poly, "hdci", c("arm", "rep", "k", "n", "rho")) |>
  filter(k == 0, arm == "phq9", B == 2000, abs(w - 0.995) < 1e-9)
fwe995 <- 100 * mean(
  (H0 |> summarise(a = any(code > 0), .by = c(rep, n)))$a)
```

## The four rules compared

The p-value rules are first examined under the null conditions of the dichotomous study, where any flag is a false positive. @tbl-null-rules shows the familywise error rate by rule and number of iterations, pooled over the four sample sizes. Three patterns stand out. Scanning all 20 items with uncorrected marginal p-values produces a familywise error rate around 60% at every $B$, which is the expected consequence of testing 20 hypotheses at $\alpha$ = .05 and the reason a correction is needed. The Westfall-Young step-down is mildly liberal at $B$ = 100, at `r nr('wy', 100)`%, falls to `r nr('wy', 200)`% at $B$ = 200, and from $B$ = 400 it is stable and slightly below its nominal 5%, between `r nr_rng('wy', 400)`% up to $B$ = 10 000. The near-zero Holm and Benjamini-Hochberg rates at $B$ = 100 and 200 are explained by the reachability floor of @eq-bhfloor: with 20 comparisons a single standout cannot be flagged below $B$ = 400. Benjamini-Hochberg can flag below that when several items sit at the Monte Carlo floor at once, which needs four of them at $B$ = 100 and two at $B$ = 200, and is rare enough under the null to leave its rate at `r nr('bh', 100)`% and `r nr('bh', 200)`%. Holm cannot, and flagged nothing. From $B$ = 400 Holm was between `r nr_rng('holm', 400)`% and Benjamini-Hochberg between `r nr_rng('bh', 400)`%.

```{r tbl-null-rules}
#| tbl-cap: "Familywise error rate of the p-value decision rules"
knitr::kable(null_rules, digits = 1,
             col.names = c("B", "Uncorrected", "Holm", "Westfall-Young",
                           "WY, joint", "Benjamini-Hochberg"))
```

*Note.* Percentages under the null conditions of the dichotomous study (20 items, no misfitting items), by number of bootstrap iterations. Pooled over the four sample sizes, `r format(n_null, big.mark = ' ')` datasets per cell. Uncorrected is the marginal p-value of @eq-pmarg. WY, joint is the Westfall-Young step-down with the observed and simulated statistics studentized together over all $B + 1$ values, computed from the same bootstrap. All values of $B$ within a replication come from one bootstrap of 10 000 iterations.

The decline of the Westfall-Young rate between $B$ = 100 and 400 is the studentization effect described in the section on bootstrap p-values. With joint studentization the rate was between `r nr_rng('wyj', 100)`% at every $B$, $B$ = 100 included. Paired within replications, the standard version exceeded the joint one by `r wjd(100)` percentage points at $B$ = 100 (SE `r wjd(100, 'se')`), by `r wjd(400)` points at $B$ = 400 (SE `r wjd(400, 'se')`), and by at most `r wjd_max_from(1000)` points from $B$ = 1000. Joint studentization therefore removes the whole decline, and the excess at small $B$ is a property of how the statistics are studentized rather than of the step-down.

What remains is a level slightly below the nominal 5% that does not change between $B$ = 400 and 10 000, under both versions. The per-item marginal tests show the same thing at their own level, flagging `r ir_rng`% of fitting items at every $B$, against the 5.0% that a valid Monte Carlo test can attain. An error that does not shrink as $B$ grows is not Monte Carlo error. It is the kind of finite-sample departure that Ferreira [-@ferreiraMethodsTestingSmall2024, Section 5] notes for bootstrap methods with estimated parameters, and here it is conservative. It was smaller in the polytomous studies, whose Westfall-Young rates under the null were between `r pw_rng`% from $B$ = 400.

The reachability floor also shapes detection. With a single misfitting item at $n$ = 150, Benjamini-Hochberg detection across $B$ = 100 to 2000 was `r sq(1, "bh")`%, jumping exactly where $B$ crosses the floor of 400. With three misfitting items the sequence was `r sq(3, "bh")`%, with substantial detection already at $B$ = 200, because three p-values at the Monte Carlo floor lower the attainable adjusted p-value to $m/(3(B+1))$. Holm detected nothing below its floor in either condition (`r sq(1, "holm")`% and `r sq(3, "holm")`%), since several standouts do not lower it. The Westfall-Young rule was flat across the whole range at `r sq(1, "wy")`% and `r sq(3, "wy")`% respectively, since it needs only $B \geq 20$ to reject and its power does not depend on $B$ beyond that.

```{r fig-rules}
#| fig-cap: "Detection and false positives for the four decision rules"
#| fig-width: 8.5
#| fig-height: 4.8
r5 |>
  mutate(metric = ifelse(is_mis, "Detection (%)", "False positives (%)")) |>
  summarise(pct = 100 * mean(flag, na.rm = TRUE),
            .by = c(rule, cond, B, metric)) |>
  mutate(rule = factor(rule, levels = c("Westfall-Young", "Benjamini-Hochberg",
                                        "Interval, w = .999", "Marginal p"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(factor(B), pct, colour = rule, linetype = rule, shape = rule,
             group = rule)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  facet_grid(metric ~ cond, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_bw("Decision rule", colours = pal_rules) +
  labs(x = "Bootstrap iterations (B)", y = NULL) +
  theme_paper(13) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.key.width = grid::unit(1.6, "cm")) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2), shape = guide_legend(nrow = 2),
         linetype = guide_legend(nrow = 2))
```

*Note.* Detection rate (misfitting items) and false positive rate (fitting items) at the anchored misfit level, by number of iterations, item set, and sample size. Rates are averaged over the misfitting-item conditions. Note the different y-axis scales for the two rows.

@fig-rules compares all four rules at the anchored misfit level. Against the interval at $w$ = .999 the Westfall-Young rule detects substantially more misfit, by `r rng(g999)` percentage points across the non-saturated nine-item conditions at $B$ = 2000, at a false positive rate of `r fpv("Westfall-Young")`% against `r fpv("Interval, w = .999")`% for the interval, pooled across arms, so it detects more at a higher cost. Part of this raw gain, however, reflects the interval's implicit error rate rather than the method. By @eq-fwer, $w$ = .999 corresponds to a familywise rate of only 0.9% for nine items, so the interval is operating far below the $\alpha$ = .05 of the p-value rules.

A fair comparison holds the error rate constant. For nine items, $w$ = .995 implies a familywise rate of 4.4% by @eq-fwer, and its observed null rate at $B$ = 2000 was `r sprintf("%.1f", fwe995)`%, closely matching the p-value rules. Against this matched interval the Westfall-Young rule still detected more misfit in every non-saturated condition, by `r rng(g995)` percentage points, with slightly fewer false positives. The remaining advantage comes from studentization and from using the joint distribution of the item statistics. More important than its size is what the matching exercise reveals: an interval width that matches a chosen $\alpha$ must be solved from @eq-fwer for each item count, and for most item counts no convenient width exists. The Westfall-Young rule targets $\alpha$ directly, whatever the number of items.

Holm, computed from the same marginal p-values, is the second FWER procedure in the comparison, and @tbl-rules-appendix reports it by condition. At $B$ = 100 it detected `r sprintf("%.1f", holm100)`% of the misfitting items, since the floor of @eq-bhfloor is `r 9 / 0.05` iterations for nine items and `r 15 / 0.05` for fifteen. At $B$ = 2000 the Westfall-Young rule detected between `r hg_rng` percentage points more than Holm across conditions, paired within replications, with standard errors of up to `r hg_se` points, and the pooled false positive rates were `r fpv("Westfall-Young")`% against `r sprintf("%.1f", fp2000_h)`%. Using the joint distribution of the item statistics therefore adds little power here, as Ferreira's [-@ferreiraMethodsTestingSmall2024] account leads one to expect for statistics that are close to independent. The practical advantage of the step-down over Holm is that it needs no minimum number of iterations.

A short scale tests Benjamini-Hochberg where the floor does not bind at all. At five items the floor is `r floor(5 / 0.05)` iterations, so the procedure operates freely at every $B$ examined, and the comparison is no longer handicapped by reachability. At $n$ = 250 it detected the misfitting item in `r bh5(250, "det_bh")`% of replications against `r bh5(250, "det_wy")`% for the Westfall-Young rule, with false positives of `r bh5(250, "fp_bh")`% against `r bh5(250, "fp_wy")`%. At $n$ = 600 both detected it in every replication, with false positives of `r bh5(600, "fp_bh")`% against `r bh5(600, "fp_wy")`%. Paired within replications, the detection difference was within one standard error of zero at both sample sizes while the false positive difference exceeded four. The preference for the Westfall-Young rule is therefore not an artifact of testing Benjamini-Hochberg only where its floor binds.

Benjamini-Hochberg and Westfall-Young performed similarly with a single misfitting item, while with several misfitting items Benjamini-Hochberg detected somewhat more, as expected since the false discovery rate is a more permissive criterion when true effects are present. The price appears on the other side of the ledger, with pooled false positives of `r fpv("Benjamini-Hochberg")`% against `r fpv("Westfall-Young")`% at $B$ = 2000, roughly a doubling. The marginal p-value, finally, is close to its nominal level per item under the null, at `r ir_rng`% of fitting items in the dichotomous study, but unusable as a screening rule. Once items misfit its false positive rate on the fitting items rises, which the section on error rates under misfit returns to. Taken together, these results support the Westfall-Young p-value as the default among the decision rules examined, with Holm a close alternative once $B$ clears its floor, the marginal p-value reserved for a single pre-specified item, and Benjamini-Hochberg for longer instruments where a false discovery criterion is acceptable and $B$ clears the reachability floor. The interval retains descriptive value, which the Discussion returns to.

## Conditional outfit under the same rules

```{r outfit-prep}
#| include: false
R6 <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(s_stat$grid)), function(i) {
  r <- s_stat$res[[i]]
  if (is.null(r)) return(NULL)
  g <- s_stat$grid[i, c("arm", "target", "n", "rep"), drop = FALSE]
  rownames(g) <- NULL
  cbind(g, r)
})) |>
  mutate(is_mis = mis > 0 & item == mis,
         f_in  = as.integer(padj_infit  < 0.05),
         f_out = as.integer(padj_outfit < 0.05),
         f_any = as.integer(f_in == 1 | f_out == 1))

r6 <- function(v) sprintf("%.1f to %.1f", min(v), max(v))
english_n <- function(x) c("one", "two", "three", "four",
  "five", "six", "seven", "eight", "nine", "ten")[x]

# familywise error and marginal calibration under the null
null6 <- R6 |>
  filter(target == "none") |>
  summarise(infit  = as.integer(sum(f_in)  > 0),
            outfit = as.integer(sum(f_out) > 0),
            union  = as.integer(sum(f_any) > 0), .by = c(arm, n, rep)) |>
  summarise(across(c(infit, outfit, union), \(x) 100 * mean(x)), .by = c(arm, n))
marg6 <- R6 |>
  filter(target == "none") |>
  summarise(infit = 100 * mean(p_infit < 0.05),
            outfit = 100 * mean(p_outfit < 0.05), .by = c(arm, n))
mcse6 <- 100 * sqrt(0.05 * 0.95 / 250)

# achieved misfit on both scales
inj6 <- R6 |>
  filter(is_mis) |>
  summarise(infit = mean(infit_msq), outfit = mean(outfit_msq), .by = arm)
inj <- function(a, s) sprintf("%.2f", inj6[[s]][inj6$arm == a])

# detection and paired discordance on the misfitting item
det6 <- R6 |>
  filter(is_mis) |>
  summarise(det_in = 100 * mean(f_in), det_out = 100 * mean(f_out),
            only_in = sum(f_in == 1 & f_out == 0),
            only_out = sum(f_in == 0 & f_out == 1),
            reps = n(), .by = c(arm, target, n))
n_win <- sum(det6$det_out > det6$det_in)          # conditions where outfit wins
gap6 <- det6$det_in - det6$det_out
gap_on  <- gap6[det6$target == "on"]
gap_off <- gap6[det6$target == "off"]

# null variability of the two statistics, and how it grows off target
sd6 <- R6 |>
  filter(target == "none") |>
  summarise(ratio = sd(outfit_msq) / sd(infit_msq), .by = c(arm, n))
sdr <- function(a) sprintf("%.1f", mean(sd6$ratio[sd6$arm == a]))
sd_loc <- R6 |>
  filter(target == "none", arm == "dich20", n == 600) |>
  mutate(loc = abs(s_stat$arms$dich20$locs[item])) |>
  summarise(ratio = sd(outfit_msq) / sd(infit_msq), loc = first(loc), .by = item)
sd_cen <- sprintf("%.1f", mean(sd_loc$ratio[rank(sd_loc$loc) <= 5]))
sd_ext <- sprintf("%.1f", mean(sd_loc$ratio[rank(-sd_loc$loc) <= 5]))
```

Every result so far concerns conditional infit. The same bootstrap produces conditional outfit at no additional cost, and the decision rules are indifferent to which statistic they are given, so it is worth asking whether anything is gained by reading both. Outfit is also widely reported in its unconditional form, for example by RUMM2030, a widely used Rasch analysis software package. The comparison here concerns conditional outfit only, and its results do not carry over to the unconditional statistic, whose behavior under the model differs [@muller_item_2020]. Johansson [-@johansson_detecting_2025] compared conditional infit and outfit for dichotomous items under the interval rule and found outfit worse throughout. The sixth study revisits that comparison under the corrected p-value and extends it to polytomous items. The two item sets were placed at correlations that inject comparable infit, `r inj("dich20", "infit")` for the dichotomous set and `r inj("phq9", "infit")` for the phq9 set, both inside the range the real phq9 items reach. A single misfitting item was placed either near the person mean or off target, the Westfall-Young rule was applied at $B$ = 1000 and $\alpha$ = .05, and both statistics were read from the same bootstrap within each replication.

Under the null conditions the FWER was `r r6(null6$outfit)`% for outfit against `r r6(null6$infit)`% for infit, across the four combinations of item set and sample size, with a Monte Carlo standard error of `r sprintf("%.1f", mcse6)` points. The marginal rates before the step-down were `r r6(marg6$outfit)`% and `r r6(marg6$infit)`%. Neither the statistic nor the correction is miscalibrated, so the studentized maximum needs no modification when the statistic it is given changes.

Detection is a different matter. Infit detected the misfitting item more often than outfit in every one of the `r english_n(nrow(det6))` conditions, and @tbl-outfit gives the margins. The gap is not small, ranging from `r sprintf("%.0f", min(gap6))` to `r sprintf("%.0f", max(gap6))` percentage points. Outfit is the unweighted mean of squared standardized residuals and is conventionally expected to earn its place on items far from the person mean, and the injected outfit is indeed larger there. Detection nevertheless moves the other way. Averaged over item sets and sample sizes the infit advantage was `r sprintf("%.0f", mean(gap_on))` points for the on-target item and `r sprintf("%.0f", mean(gap_off))` points for the off-target one. The null conditions explain why. Outfit is the more variable statistic under a true model, by a factor of `r sdr("dich20")` in the dichotomous set and `r sdr("phq9")` in the phq9 set, and within the dichotomous set that factor is `r sd_cen` for the five most central items and `r sd_ext` for the five most extreme. The variance grows faster than the signal exactly where outfit was expected to help.

Because both statistics come from the same bootstrap, the comparison can be made replication by replication rather than only on the margins. @tbl-outfit reports the discordant counts. Replications in which outfit flagged the misfitting item and infit did not never exceeded `r max(det6$only_out)` of 250, against up to `r max(det6$only_in)` in the other direction, and every condition favours infit at $p$ < .01 by an exact test on the discordant pairs. In these conditions outfit added little to what infit detected.

This has a direct consequence for practice, because both statistics often appear side by side in the standard output. Flagging an item when either statistic is significant tests 2$k$ hypotheses while each correction covers $k$, and the null FWER of that combined rule was `r r6(null6$union)`%, against a nominal 5% and the `r r6(c(null6$infit, null6$outfit))`% the two statistics reach on their own. The inflation is below the doubling that independent statistics would produce, since the two are computed on the same responses and are positively dependent, but it is real and adds almost no detection. For conditional statistics at these settings, the results favor deciding on infit and treating outfit as descriptive.

```{r tbl-outfit}
#| tbl-cap: "Detection and paired disagreement, conditional infit versus outfit"
det6 |>
  mutate(Items = ifelse(arm == "dich20", "20 dich", "9 phq9"),
         Target = ifelse(target == "on", "On target", "Off target"),
         p = mapply(function(a, b) if (a + b == 0L) NA_real_ else
                      stats::binom.test(a, a + b, 0.5)$p.value,
                    only_out, only_in),
         p = ifelse(is.na(p), "-", ifelse(p < 0.001, "< .001", sprintf("%.3f", p)))) |>
  arrange(Items, desc(Target), n) |>
  select(Items, Target, n, det_in, det_out, only_in, only_out, p) |>
  collapse_keys(c("Items", "Target")) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1, align = "llrrrrrr",
               col.names = c("Items", "Target", "n", "Det infit", "Det outfit",
                             "Only infit", "Only outfit", "p"))
```

*Note.* Westfall-Young rule at $B$ = 1000 and $\alpha$ = .05, 250 replications per condition. Det is the percentage of replications in which the misfitting item was flagged. Only infit and Only outfit count the replications in which one statistic flagged it and the other did not. The p-value is an exact binomial test on those discordant counts. Design and false positive rates are in @tbl-outfit-appendix.

## Random responding under the same rules

```{r mech-prep}
#| include: false
mism <- s_mech$mis
LH <- bind_part(s_mech, "hdci", c("rep", "k", "n")) |>
  filter(abs(w - 0.999) < 1e-9) |>
  mutate(mech = "noise") |> select(mech, rep, k, n, B, item, code)
LP <- bind_part(s_mech, "pval", c("rep", "k", "n")) |>
  mutate(mech = "noise") |> select(mech, rep, k, n, B, item, padj_fwer)
XH <- bind_part(s_poly, "hdci", c("arm", "rep", "k", "n", "rho")) |>
  filter(arm == "phq9", abs(rho - 0.85) < 1e-9, abs(w - 0.999) < 1e-9) |>
  mutate(mech = "dim") |> select(mech, rep, k, n, B, item, code)
XP <- bind_part(s_poly, "pval", c("arm", "rep", "k", "n", "rho")) |>
  filter(arm == "phq9", abs(rho - 0.85) < 1e-9) |>
  mutate(mech = "dim") |> select(mech, rep, k, n, B, item, padj_fwer)

# false positives on the fitting items, two misfitting items, n = 1000, B = 2000
fp_h <- bind_rows(LH, XH) |>
  filter(k == 2, n == 1000, B == 2000, !(item %in% mism)) |>
  summarise(fp = 100 * mean(code > 0), .by = mech)
fp_p <- bind_rows(LP, XP) |>
  filter(k == 2, n == 1000, B == 2000, !(item %in% mism)) |>
  summarise(fp = 100 * mean(padj_fwer < al5, na.rm = TRUE), .by = mech)
mq <- function(d, m) sprintf("%.1f", d$fp[d$mech == m])

# direction of the false flags under the interval rule, pooled over conditions
dir_m <- bind_rows(LH, XH) |>
  filter(k > 0, !(item %in% mism), code > 0) |>
  summarise(over = 100 * mean(code == 1), .by = mech)
oq <- function(m) sprintf("%.0f", dir_m$over[dir_m$mech == m])

# detection of the two target items at n = 250
det_m <- bind_rows(LP, XP) |>
  filter(k == 2, n == 250, B == 2000, item %in% mism) |>
  summarise(det = 100 * mean(padj_fwer < al5, na.rm = TRUE), .by = mech)
dq <- function(m) sprintf("%.1f", det_m$det[det_m$mech == m])
```

Every result so far induces misfit through multidimensionality, so two of them could in principle be properties of that mechanism rather than of misfit in general. The first is the false positives that appear on fitting items once misfitting items are present. The second is the masking that weakens detection when two items misfit together. The mechanism check separates the two. It holds the item set, the conditions and the decision rules fixed, and replaces multidimensionality with random responding at matched infit.

The false positives are not specific to multidimensionality. With two misfitting items at $n$ = 1000 and $B$ = 2000, random responding produced false positives on the seven fitting items of `r mq(fp_h, "noise")`% under the interval rule at $w$ = .999 and `r mq(fp_p, "noise")`% under the Westfall-Young rule, against `r mq(fp_h, "dim")`% and `r mq(fp_p, "dim")`% under multidimensionality. Nearly all false flags pointed in the overfit direction under the interval rule for both mechanisms, at `r oq("noise")`% and `r oq("dim")`% of flags. Direction is read from the band, so the p-value rules cannot be scored the same way. What puts a fitting item outside its expected range is contamination of the total score that it is conditioned on, rather than the particular way that contamination arises. The error rate results are therefore not an artifact of the mechanism, and the multidimensional condition is the more forgiving of the two.

Masking is mechanism-specific, and should be read as such. Two independently noisy items do not mask each other, and detection of the two target items at $n$ = 250 was `r dq("noise")`% under random responding against `r dq("dim")`% under multidimensionality. Masking requires the misfitting items to share a source. That is the case worth planning for, since a secondary dimension rarely involves a single item, but it is not a property of misfit in general.

## Error rates when some items misfit

```{r partial-prep}
#| include: false
# Familywise error over the fitting items (any fitting item flagged) and the
# false discovery proportion, per replication, at B = 2000, for every
# condition with misfitting items. Holm is computed from the marginal p-values
# where the study stored them (not in the mechanism check).
per_rep_err <- function(L, keys) {
  L |>
    summarise(fp = sum(flag[!is_mis]), tp = sum(flag[is_mis]),
              .by = all_of(c(keys, "rep", "rule"))) |>
    mutate(any_fp = fp > 0, fdp = ifelse(fp + tp > 0, fp / (fp + tp), 0)) |>
    summarise(fwer = 100 * mean(any_fp), fdr = 100 * mean(fdp),
              .by = all_of(c(keys, "rule")))
}
# polytomous studies at the anchored level
PE <- r5_all |>
  filter(B == 2000, !is.na(flag)) |>
  per_rep_err(c("arm", "k", "n")) |>
  mutate(set = ifelse(arm == "phq9", "9 phq9", "15 polytomous"))
# dichotomous study (rho = .15), fresh data
GPm <- GP |>
  filter(k > 0, B == 2000) |>
  mutate(p_holm = p.adjust(p_marg, "holm"), .by = c(rep, k, n, B),
         is_mis = mapply(function(k, it) it %in% s_grid$misfit[seq_len(k)], k, item))
DE <- bind_rows(
  GPm |> transmute(k, n, rep, item, is_mis, rule = "Holm", flag = p_holm < al5),
  GPm |> transmute(k, n, rep, item, is_mis, rule = "Westfall-Young", flag = padj_fwer < al5),
  GPm |> transmute(k, n, rep, item, is_mis, rule = "Benjamini-Hochberg", flag = padj_bh < al5)
) |>
  per_rep_err(c("k", "n")) |>
  mutate(set = "20 dichotomous")
# mechanism check, random responding in the phq9 set
ME <- bind_part(s_mech, "pval", c("rep", "k", "n")) |>
  filter(B == 2000) |>
  mutate(is_mis = mapply(function(k, it) it %in% mism[seq_len(k)], k, item))
ME <- bind_rows(
  ME |> transmute(k, n, rep, item, is_mis, rule = "Westfall-Young", flag = padj_fwer < al5),
  ME |> transmute(k, n, rep, item, is_mis, rule = "Benjamini-Hochberg", flag = padj_bh < al5)
) |>
  filter(!is.na(flag)) |>
  per_rep_err(c("k", "n")) |>
  mutate(set = "9 phq9, random responding")
partial <- bind_rows(PE |> select(-arm), DE, ME) |>
  filter(rule %in% c("Holm", "Westfall-Young", "Benjamini-Hochberg"))
pe <- function(set_, k_, n_, rule_, col = "fwer") sprintf("%.1f",
  partial[[col]][partial$set == set_ & partial$k == k_ & partial$n == n_ &
                   partial$rule == rule_])
pe_rng <- function(set_, rule_, col, nmax) {
  v <- partial[[col]][partial$set %in% set_ & partial$rule == rule_ & partial$n <= nmax]
  sprintf("%.1f and %.1f", min(v), max(v))
}
# per-item false positive rate of the uncorrected marginal p-value on fitting
# items, phq9 at the anchored level, n = 1000, B = 2000
marg_fp <- r5_all |>
  filter(arm == "phq9", n == 1000, B == 2000, rule == "Marginal p", !is_mis) |>
  summarise(fp = 100 * mean(flag), .by = k)
mfp <- function(k_) sprintf("%.1f", marg_fp$fp[marg_fp$k == k_])
# Westfall-Young over fitting items at the strongest polytomous misfit level
wy75 <- bind_part(s_poly, "pval", c("arm", "rep", "k", "n", "rho")) |>
  filter(abs(rho - 0.75) < 1e-9, k > 0, B == 2000) |>
  mutate(is_mis = mapply(function(a, k, it) it %in% mis5(a, k), arm, k, item)) |>
  summarise(any = any(padj_fwer[!is_mis] < al5), .by = c(arm, k, n, rep)) |>
  summarise(pct = 100 * mean(any), .by = c(arm, k, n))
```
