The error rates reported so far were measured under the null, where every item fits. With misfitting items present, the error rate that strong FWER control concerns is the probability of flagging at least one of the fitting items, and the error rate that Benjamini-Hochberg targets is the false discovery rate, the expected proportion of flagged items that in fact fit. @tbl-partial reports both for every condition with misfitting items, at $B$ = 2000.

At sample sizes of 250 or below, the rates were close to nominal. At the anchored misfit level in the polytomous sets, the Westfall-Young rate over the fitting items was between `r pe_rng(c("9 phq9", "15 polytomous"), "Westfall-Young", "fwer", 250)`%, and the false discovery rate of Benjamini-Hochberg between `r pe_rng(c("9 phq9", "15 polytomous"), "Benjamini-Hochberg", "fdr", 250)`%. At $n$ = 1000 every procedure exceeded its nominal level. For the nine phq9 items, the Westfall-Young rate over fitting items was `r pe("9 phq9", 1, 1000, "Westfall-Young")`% with one misfitting item and `r pe("9 phq9", 2, 1000, "Westfall-Young")`% with two, the Holm rate `r pe("9 phq9", 1, 1000, "Holm")`% and `r pe("9 phq9", 2, 1000, "Holm")`%, and the false discovery rate of Benjamini-Hochberg `r pe("9 phq9", 1, 1000, "Benjamini-Hochberg", "fdr")`% and `r pe("9 phq9", 2, 1000, "Benjamini-Hochberg", "fdr")`%. The rates grew with misfit severity, reaching `r sprintf("%.1f", max(wy75$pct))`% for Westfall-Young at $\rho$ = .75, and were higher under random responding, at `r pe("9 phq9, random responding", 2, 1000, "Westfall-Young")`% with two misfitting items at $n$ = 1000.

The source of the excess lies in the per-item tests rather than in the corrections. At $n$ = 1000 the uncorrected marginal p-value flagged `r mfp(1)`% of the fitting phq9 items with one misfitting item and `r mfp(2)`% with two, where a valid per-item test would flag about 5%. Each fitting item's statistic is conditioned on a total score that includes the misfitting items, so its distribution changes when they misfit, while the bootstrap reference is generated from a model in which all items fit. This is the failure of subset pivotality described in the section on bootstrap p-values, and Ferreira [-@ferreiraMethodsTestingSmall2024, p. 2] makes the underlying point that a p-value can have the wrong distribution because the model is incorrect rather than because its null hypothesis is false. It also explains why Holm, which needs no pivotality condition, failed in the same conditions, since it relies on valid marginal p-values. The procedures studied here therefore provide weak FWER control, under the complete null, and no correction applied to these per-item tests can provide strong control once misfit contaminates the conditioning score. The contamination grows with sample size and misfit severity, which is why the failure is a large-sample one, and removing the most misfitting item before judging the rest reduces it, a point the Discussion returns to.

The false discovery rate results bear on the comparison with Benjamini-Hochberg. Its false discovery rate stayed close to nominal where the per-item tests were close to valid and exceeded it where they were not, as every rule's error rate did, and the Westfall-Young rule had a false discovery rate at or below that of Benjamini-Hochberg in every condition. Benjamini-Hochberg is guaranteed to control the false discovery rate when the p-values of the true hypotheses are independent, or when the test statistics have positive regression dependency on each of the statistics of the true hypotheses [@benjamini_control_2001]. That condition covers statistics with a unidimensional latent variable distribution, but Benjamini and Yekutieli [-@benjamini_control_2001] leave open how far it extends to two-sided tests, and conditional infit is tested two-sided on a statistic computed from the residuals of the fitted model rather than on the responses themselves. Whether the condition holds here has therefore not been established, and the rates above are the evidence offered here. Resampling-based procedures that control the false discovery rate using the joint distribution of the statistics, in the spirit of the Westfall-Young step-down, also exist [@yekutieliResamplingbasedFalseDiscovery1999] and were not studied. The preference for a familywise criterion rests on the use of the analysis. A scale of 5 to 20 items is judged item by item, each flag leads to an item being considered for removal, and a single false flag changes the instrument. The false discovery rate is most useful when many hypotheses are tested and many discoveries are expected [@ferreiraMethodsTestingSmall2024], which is rarely the case in item fit analysis.

# Decision stability

The previous sections report error rates averaged over many simulated datasets. An analyst has one dataset. Because the cutoff interval and the p-values are computed from a finite simulation, two analysts who run identical analyses on the same data with different random seeds can potentially reach different conclusions. This section quantifies how often that happens. Ten datasets per condition were held fixed and each was analyzed with 25 different bootstrap seeds. Since the data are fixed, the observed infit values are fixed, and only the simulated reference distribution varies between seeds. Everything reported in this section is therefore simulation noise alone, with no contribution from sampling variability.

For each item and dataset, the flag rate $p$ is the proportion of the 25 seeds in which the item was flagged. It estimates the probability that a single analysis of that dataset flags that item. An item is counted as unstable when $0 < p < 1$, meaning the flagging decision depends on the seed. Twenty-five seeds resolve the flag rate in steps of 0.04, so an item whose flag probability is very close to 0 or to 1 will usually appear perfectly stable, and the unstable counts below are best read as lower bounds.

The quantity that matters to an analyst is whether a second run would flag the same set of items. Two analyses with different seeds disagree when their sets of flagged items differ, and with 25 seeds per dataset the probability of this can be measured directly as the proportion of the 300 pairs of seeds that disagree,

$$
D = 1 - \frac{\sum_j \binom{c_j}{2}}{\binom{S}{2}},
$$ {#eq-disagree}

where $c_j$ is the number of seeds that produced the $j$-th distinct set of flagged items and $S$ = 25 is the number of seeds. $D$ is computed within each dataset and averaged over the ten datasets of a condition, and it needs no assumption about how the items depend on each other. For a single item the corresponding probability is $2p(1 - p)$, the chance that one of two seeds flags the item and the other does not. It is largest, at 0.5, for an item flagged in half the seeds and falls to zero at either extreme, so it measures how close an item is to the decision boundary.

```{r stab-prep}
#| include: false
al <- 0.05
SP <- bind_part(s_stab, "pval", c("arm", "k", "rho", "n", "dataset", "seed")) |>
  mutate(rho = round(rho, 2))
SH <- bind_part(s_stab, "hdci", c("arm", "k", "rho", "n", "dataset", "seed")) |>
  filter(abs(w - 0.999) < 1e-9) |>
  mutate(rho = round(rho, 2))

rate_p <- SP |>
  summarise(p = mean(padj_fwer < al, na.rm = TRUE),
            .by = c(arm, k, rho, n, B, dataset, item)) |>
  mutate(rule = "FWER p-value")
rate_h <- SH |>
  summarise(p = mean(code > 0), .by = c(arm, k, rho, n, B, dataset, item)) |>
  mutate(rule = "Interval, w = .999")
rates <- bind_rows(rate_p, rate_h)

# pooled unstable percentages, anchored misfit (rho = .85, both arms and n)
pool85 <- rates |>
  filter(rho == 0.85, k > 0) |>
  summarise(pct = 100 * mean(p > 0 & p < 1), .by = c(rule, B))
pf <- function(rule_, B_) sprintf("%.1f", pool85$pct[pool85$rule == rule_ & pool85$B == B_])

# pooled null (no misfitting items)
pool0 <- rates |>
  filter(k == 0, rule == "FWER p-value") |>
  summarise(pct = 100 * mean(p > 0 & p < 1), .by = B)

# dataset-cluster bootstrap SE for the pooled anchored estimates (FWER)
set.seed(11)
p85f <- rates |> filter(rho == 0.85, k > 0, rule == "FWER p-value") |>
  mutate(cl = paste(arm, n, dataset))
boot_pool <- function(B_) {
  x <- p85f[p85f$B == B_, ]
  cls <- unique(x$cl)
  sd(replicate(300, {
    cs <- sample(cls, replace = TRUE)
    y <- do.call(rbind, lapply(cs, function(cc) x[x$cl == cc, ]))
    100 * mean(y$p > 0 & y$p < 1)
  }))
}
se400 <- boot_pool(400); se2000 <- boot_pool(2000)

# two-analyst disagreement measured from seed pairs (Equation 5): the share of
# the choose(S, 2) pairs of seeds whose sets of flagged items differ. Seeds
# with a missing item result are dropped. The independence product with the
# finite-seed correction S / (S - 1) is kept for comparison.
skeys <- c("rule", "arm", "k", "rho", "n", "B", "dataset")
SF <- bind_rows(
  SP |> transmute(arm, k, rho, n, dataset, seed, B, item,
                  rule = "FWER p-value", flag = as.integer(padj_fwer < al)),
  SH |> transmute(arm, k, rho, n, dataset, seed, B, item,
                  rule = "Interval, w = .999", flag = as.integer(code > 0))
) |>
  filter(!any(is.na(flag)), .by = all_of(c(skeys, "seed")))
D_emp <- SF |>
  arrange(item) |>
  summarise(pat = paste(flag, collapse = ""), .by = all_of(c(skeys, "seed"))) |>
  summarise(S = n(), D = 1 - sum(choose(table(pat), 2)) / choose(n(), 2),
            .by = all_of(skeys))
D_ind <- SF |>
  summarise(p = mean(flag), S = n(), .by = all_of(c(skeys, "item"))) |>
  summarise(D_ind = 1 - prod(1 - 2 * p * (1 - p) * S / (S - 1)),
            .by = all_of(skeys))
D_all <- left_join(D_emp, D_ind, by = skeys)
stopifnot(nrow(D_all) == nrow(D_emp), all(D_emp$S >= 20))

# pooled two-analyst disagreement (FWER), anchored misfit
dis <- D_all |>
  filter(rho == 0.85, k > 0, rule == "FWER p-value") |>
  summarise(pct = 100 * mean(D), pct_ind = 100 * mean(D_ind), .by = B) |>
  arrange(B)
dv <- setNames(sprintf("%.0f", dis$pct), dis$B)
dis_gap <- sprintf("%.1f", max(abs(dis$pct - dis$pct_ind)))
# where independence fails: datasets in which the independence product
# overstates or understates the measured disagreement by more than 5 points
dep <- D_all |>
  filter(k > 0) |>
  summarise(N = n(), over = sum(D_ind - D > 0.05), under = sum(D_ind - D < -0.05),
            maxgap = 100 * max(abs(D_ind - D)), .by = rule)
dq_ <- function(rule_, col) dep[[col]][dep$rule == rule_]
# disagreement at B = 2000 across all misfit conditions (FWER)
dis_cond <- D_all |>
  filter(k > 0, rule == "FWER p-value", B == 2000) |>
  summarise(pct = 100 * mean(D), .by = c(arm, rho, n))

# borderline-item counts per dataset at the strongest misfit, B = 2000
bord <- rate_p |>
  filter(B == 2000, rho == 0.15, k > 0) |>
  summarise(nb = sum(p > 0 & p < 1), .by = c(arm, n, dataset)) |>
  summarise(mb = mean(nb), .by = c(arm, n))
bb <- function(n_) sprintf("%.1f", mean(bord$mb[bord$n == n_]))

# unstable % per condition for the figure
unst <- rates |>
  filter(k > 0) |>
  summarise(pct = 100 * mean(p > 0 & p < 1), .by = c(rule, arm, rho, n, B))
```

Under the null conditions, flagging with the Westfall-Young p-value is essentially reproducible. Pooled across both item sets and sample sizes, `r sprintf("%.1f", pool0$pct[pool0$B == 100])`% of items had a seed-dependent flag at $B$ = 100, `r sprintf("%.1f", pool0$pct[pool0$B == 400])`% at $B$ = 400, and none at $B$ = 2000. At the anchored misfit level ($\rho$ = .85), pooled the same way, `r pf("FWER p-value", 400)`% of items were unstable at $B$ = 400 and `r pf("FWER p-value", 2000)`% at $B$ = 2000, with a Monte Carlo standard error of `r sprintf("%.1f", max(se400, se2000))` percentage points. The interval rule at $w$ = .999 was consistently less stable, with `r pf("Interval, w = .999", 400)`% unstable items at $B$ = 400 and `r pf("Interval, w = .999", 2000)`% at $B$ = 2000. The two-analyst disagreement probability shows that more iterations keep helping beyond the point where error rates have converged. Pooled at the anchored level, the probability that two seeds using the Westfall-Young rule disagree about at least one item was `r dv["100"]`% at $B$ = 100, `r dv["400"]`% at $B$ = 400, `r dv["1000"]`% at $B$ = 1000, and `r dv["2000"]`% at $B$ = 2000. In other words, $B$ = 400 is where the error rates are trustworthy, but reproducibility keeps improving well past it.

Treating the items as if they flipped independently gives nearly the same pooled values, within `r dis_gap` percentage points, once each item's $2p(1 - p)$ is multiplied by $S/(S - 1)$ to remove the bias of estimating $p$ from 25 seeds. The average hides where independence fails. For the Westfall-Young rule the independence product overstated the measured disagreement by more than 5 percentage points in `r dq_("FWER p-value", "over")` of `r dq_("FWER p-value", "N")` combinations of dataset and number of iterations, by up to `r sprintf("%.0f", dq_("FWER p-value", "maxgap"))` points, and `r if (dq_("FWER p-value", "under") == 0) "never understated it by as much" else paste("understated it by as much in", dq_("FWER p-value", "under"))`. In those datasets one seed's maximum statistic moves several decisions together, the coupling that the step-down introduces. For the interval rule, whose items are judged separately, the two agreed within `r sprintf("%.0f", dq_("Interval, w = .999", "maxgap"))` points in every dataset.

```{r fig-stability}
#| fig-cap: "Seed dependence of flagging decisions"
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.5
unst |>
  mutate(rho = factor(sprintf("%.2f", rho))) |>
  ggplot(aes(factor(B), pct, colour = rho, shape = rho, linetype = rule,
             group = interaction(rho, rule))) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  facet_grid(arm ~ n, labeller = label_both) +
  scale_bw("Correlation", colours = rev(pal_ramp3), linetype = FALSE) +
  scale_linetype_manual(name = "Decision rule", values = c("solid", "42")) +
  labs(x = "Bootstrap iterations (B)", y = "Items with seed-dependent flag (%)") +
  theme_paper(12) +
  theme(legend.key.width = grid::unit(1.4, "cm"))
```

*Note.* Percentage of items whose flagging decision depends on the bootstrap seed (25 seeds per dataset, 10 datasets per condition), by number of iterations, misfit severity, decision rule, item set, and sample size. Lower values of the inter-dimensional correlation mean stronger misfit. Per-condition values carry Monte Carlo standard errors of up to about 3 percentage points and are tabulated in @tbl-stab-appendix.

@fig-stability shows the full pattern, and its most striking feature is that instability is not monotone in misfit severity or sample size. The strongest misfit ($\rho$ = .15) produces the most instability at $n$ = 250 but none at all at $n$ = 1000, where every item is flagged or cleared decisively in every seed. The explanation is the number of items sitting near the decision boundary. At $B$ = 2000 the strongest misfit condition leaves on average `r bb(250)` items per dataset with a seed-dependent flag at $n$ = 250, but `r bb(1000)` at $n$ = 1000. Instability arises where the evidence about an item is strong enough to approach the flagging threshold but not strong enough to pass it clearly, and it is the number of such boundary items, not the severity of misfit or the sample size as such, that drives it. With ten datasets per condition, the stability results describe the datasets drawn and are best read as an illustration of this dependence rather than as rates that carry over to other data. At $B$ = 2000 the probability that two seeds disagreed ranged from `r sprintf("%.0f", min(dis_cond$pct))` to `r sprintf("%.0f", max(dis_cond$pct))`% across the misfit conditions, according to how many items lay near the threshold.

All of this instability is simulation noise, since the data are held fixed. How much of it an analysis shows, however, is set by the data. If an item's p-value with unlimited iterations is $\pi$, its Monte Carlo estimate from $B$ iterations has a standard error of about $\sqrt{\pi(1 - \pi)/B}$, so the number of iterations needed to make the decision reproducible grows with the inverse square of the distance between $\pi$ and $\alpha$. For items whose p-values lie close to the threshold no affordable number of iterations removes the instability, and how many such items a dataset has is a property of the dataset. Seed sensitivity is then best understood as a diagnostic. If re-running an analysis with a different seed changes which items are flagged, the affected items are borderline cases whose evidence lies close to the threshold, and they need more data or substantive judgment rather than a luckier seed. Reporting the number of iterations and the seed alongside item fit results makes this visible to readers. The Westfall-Young p-value is preferable to the interval rule on this criterion as well, and the interval rule's instability at $w$ = .999 declines only slowly with $B$, consistent with its extreme quantiles remaining poorly estimated throughout the practical range.

# Discussion

```{r disc-prep}
#| include: false
# relative interval width at ten simulated values per tail, for the widths
# where the grid contains the matching number of iterations
dpt10 <- relw |>
  summarise(m = median(rel), .by = c(w, B)) |>
  filter(abs((1 - w) / 2 * B - 10) < 1e-9)
dpt_short <- sprintf("%.0f", 100 * (1 - min(dpt10$m)))

# null familywise error of the Westfall-Young rule, dichotomous study
wyq <- function(B_) sprintf("%.1f", null_rules$wy[null_rules$B == B_])

# Westfall-Young null rate from B = 400 by item set, pooled over n
wy_k <- bind_rows(
  null_any |> filter(B >= 400) |> summarise(pct = 100 * mean(wy), .by = B) |>
    mutate(set = "20 dichotomous"),
  bind_part(s_poly, "pval", c("arm", "rep", "k", "n", "rho")) |>
    filter(k == 0, B >= 400) |>
    summarise(any = any(padj_fwer < al5, na.rm = TRUE), .by = c(arm, rep, n, B)) |>
    summarise(pct = 100 * mean(any), .by = c(arm, B)) |> rename(set = arm),
  P7 |> filter(k == 0, B >= 400) |>
    summarise(any = any(padj_fwer < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE), .by = c(rep, n, B)) |>
    summarise(pct = 100 * mean(any), .by = B) |> mutate(set = "5 polytomous")
)
wy_k_rng <- sprintf("%.1f and %.1f", min(wy_k$pct), max(wy_k$pct))

# Westfall-Young detection at the anchored misfit level, B = 2000
det_wy <- RP |>
  mutate(is_mis = mapply(function(a, k, it) it %in% mis5(a, k), arm, k, item)) |>
  filter(is_mis, B == 2000)
pc1 <- function(x) sub("\\.0$", "", sprintf("%.1f", x))  # 100.0 prints as 100
dwy <- function(a, n_, k_) pc1(100 * mean(
  det_wy$padj_fwer[det_wy$arm == a & det_wy$n == n_ &
                     det_wy$k == k_] < al5, na.rm = TRUE))
dwyi <- function(a, n_, k_, it) pc1(100 * mean(
  det_wy$padj_fwer[det_wy$arm == a & det_wy$n == n_ & det_wy$k == k_ &
                     det_wy$item == it] < al5, na.rm = TRUE))

# settings implied by a familywise error rate of .05, by number of comparisons
alpha_rec <- 0.05
rec <- data.frame(m = c(5, 10, 15, 20, 30))
rec$w     <- (1 - alpha_rec)^(1 / rec$m)
rec$B_int <- signif(20 / (1 - rec$w), 2)
rec$B_bh  <- floor(rec$m / alpha_rec)
rec$B_wy  <- floor(1 / alpha_rec)

fmt_n <- function(x) format(x, big.mark = " ", scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE)
recq  <- function(col, m_) fmt_n(rec[[col]][rec$m == m_])
wq    <- function(m_) sub("^0", "", sprintf("%.5f", rec$w[rec$m == m_]))
# Benjamini-Hochberg reachability floor at any number of comparisons
bhf   <- function(m_) fmt_n(floor(m_ / alpha_rec))
```

This paper asked how the interval width and the number of bootstrap iterations should be chosen for simulation-based cutoffs, and whether the interval is the best way to turn a bootstrap into a decision about item fit. The answers are connected. The width is the FWER parameter of the interval rule and is described well by @eq-fwer. The number of iterations required is set by the width, and not by the sample size that the earlier guidance conditioned on. The same bootstrap also supports a p-value rule that targets a chosen error rate directly, detects more misfit at a matched error rate, and needs far fewer iterations.

## Recommendations for practice

Five recommendations follow from the results.

1. **Decide with the corrected p-value.** Among the decision rules examined, the Westfall-Young step-down at $\alpha$ = .05 performed best, and it is the recommended decision rule for conditional item fit. Its FWER under the null was at or slightly below the nominal level from $B$ = 400 onward. Holm gave nearly the same results once $B$ cleared its floor of $k/\alpha$ iterations, but the step-down needs no such floor. It also detected more misfit than the interval rule at a matched error rate, and it was the more stable of the two under reseeding. Against Benjamini-Hochberg it holds up even where that procedure is unconstrained: on a five-item scale, whose reachability floor of `r bhf(5)` iterations binds at no $B$ examined here, the two detected the misfitting item equally often while Benjamini-Hochberg flagged roughly half again as many fitting ones. Other FWER procedures were not examined. The control holds when all items fit, and once items misfit the false flags on fitting items grow with sample size for every rule, which the fifth recommendation addresses.

2. **Use at least 400 iterations, and more when computation allows.** Below 400 the Westfall-Young rule was mildly liberal under the null, at `r wyq(100)`% at $B$ = 100, an excess that comes from how the statistics are studentized and that joint studentization removes, and decisions were noticeably seed-dependent. The probability that two analysts using different seeds disagree about at least one item kept falling past that point, from `r dv["400"]`% at $B$ = 400 to `r dv["2000"]`% at $B$ = 2000, so at least 1000 to 2000 iterations are worth the cost for a final analysis.

3. **Report the interval as a description and set its width to .95.** At w = .95, `r bq(0.95)` iterations bring the interval within 1% of the width it reaches with 10 000, so the band shown to readers is close to the width it claims to be. At w = .999 the same 1% takes `r bq(0.999)` iterations, far more than is usually run, so the stated width is not the width the reader is actually seeing. A band showing where a fitting item's infit is expected to fall is worth reporting, but only when its stated width is real.

4. **Report the number of iterations and the random seed.** Both are part of the analysis. Without them a reader cannot tell whether a borderline item would have been flagged in a rerun. The seed will however only be useful if the data are also shared.

5. **Remove items one at a time.** This is the workflow recommended by Johansson [-@johansson_detecting_2025], and its sequential error rates were not evaluated here, since every reported rate refers to a single analysis. It is retained because misfitting items contaminate the total score that the other items are judged against, which is the source of the false flags on fitting items when some items misfit, and removing the most misfitting item first reduces that contamination before the remaining items are judged. Repeated testing across removal rounds adds multiplicity that the corrections studied here do not address, as the Limitations discuss.

The default settings in `easyRasch2` 1.1.0, with $w$ = .999 and $B$ = 250, show what this looks like in practice. A 99.9% interval has to contain 99.9% of the simulated values, and with the default 250 iterations that is all of them, so the interval is nothing more than the range of what the simulation happened to produce. The width setting has no effect on anything, and the error rate the analysis delivers follows from the iteration count rather than from a deliberate choice. For 20 dichotomous items, $w$ = .999 promises that a fitting item will be falsely flagged somewhere in the scale about `r pq("20 dichotomous", 0.999)`% of the time. What the simulation delivered was `r fq("20 dichotomous", 0.999, 400)`% at 400 iterations and `r fq("20 dichotomous", 0.999, 200)`% at 200, the two settings that bracket the default 250 iterations. The recommendation that follows is to base flagging on the Westfall-Young corrected p-value rather than on the interval, and to show the interval as a descriptive band at $w$ = .95. The package has since moved to these settings. From version 1.2.0, `easyRasch2` flags items on the Westfall-Young p-value, shows the interval at $w$ = .95 and runs 400 iterations by default, and its development version studentizes the observed and simulated statistics jointly, which removes the small-$B$ excess shown in @tbl-null-rules.

These recommendations are not confined to users of R. The same analyses are available through `easyRasch2jmv` [@johanssonEasyRasch2jmv2026], a module for the jamovi statistical platform [@jamovi_2026] that delegates every computation to `easyRasch2`, so that results are numerically identical given the same seeds and iteration counts. Simulation-based cutoffs can be more demanding to use than a rule of thumb, since they require a decision about the number of iterations and about which decision rule to apply, and the recommendations given here are meant to make those decisions simpler.

## Choosing the width and the number of iterations together

The second and third recommendations fix settings for a particular purpose. A width is a promise about the error rate, and the number of iterations decides whether the promise is kept. What links them is the expected number of simulated values in each tail of the interval, $(1 - w)B/2$. Across the widths studied here, roughly ten values per tail brought the interval to within `r dpt_short` percent of its width at 10 000 iterations, which corresponds to $B \approx 20/(1 - w)$. @tbl-recommendations applies this to the settings that a target error rate implies. For each number of items the width column solves @eq-fwer at a FWER of .05, and the remaining columns give the iterations that each decision rule needs in order to operate at that error rate at all.

```{r tbl-recommendations}
#| tbl-cap: "Interval width and iterations required by each decision rule"
rec |>
  transmute(Items = m,
            Width = sub("^0", "", sprintf("%.5f", w)),
            Interval = fmt_n(B_int),
            `Holm, Benjamini-Hochberg` = fmt_n(B_bh),
            `Westfall-Young` = fmt_n(B_wy)) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "rrrrr")
```

*Note.* By number of items, at a familywise error rate or false discovery rate of .05. The width solves @eq-fwer. The interval column applies the draws-per-tail rule $B$ = 20/(1 - $w$) to that width, rounded to two significant digits. The Holm, Benjamini-Hochberg column is the reachability floor of @eq-bhfloor for a single standout item, which the two procedures share, and the Westfall-Young column is 1/$\alpha$. The columns give the point at which each rule can operate at the stated error rate, not a recommended setting.

Three patterns in the table underpin the recommendations above. First, the iterations that the interval rule needs grow steeply with the number of items. Already at 20 items the required width of `r wq(20)` implies about `r recq("B_int", 20)` iterations, which is an order of magnitude beyond what is usually run, and these figures apply the draws-per-tail rule beyond the iteration counts the convergence study covered. Second, the floor of Holm and Benjamini-Hochberg grows linearly with the number of comparisons. It is a reachability constraint rather than a matter of power, so no amount of misfit compensates for too few iterations. Third, the Westfall-Young requirement does not grow at all, because the correction uses the distribution of the maximum rather than a per-comparison quantile. This is a statement about reachability only. The Monte Carlo precision of the step-down's first critical value is that of the $1 - \alpha$ quantile of the maximum, which for a fixed $\alpha$ depends on $B$ rather than directly on the number of items, and in the simulations the null rate from $B$ = 400 was between `r wy_k_rng` percent across the 5, 9, 15 and 20-item sets, with no trend in the number of items. Reproducibility at the scale level is another matter, since more items mean more items that can lie near the threshold, and the stability study covers 9 and 15 items only.

The last column is not a recommendation, which is why the second recommendation in the list above asks for far more than 20 iterations. Those iterations make a rejection possible, but they do not make a decision reproducible. Error rates and reproducibility are separate requirements, and it is the latter that sets the number of iterations worth running in practice.

## What changes for the earlier recommendations

The recommendation of 100 to 400 parametric bootstrap iterations in Johansson [-@johansson_detecting_2025], scaled by sample size, should be replaced by a number chosen from the decision rule. Sample size does not play a role here. For the interval rule the requirement follows from the width, and the width that delivers a chosen error rate follows in turn from the number of items, so the iterations needed rise steeply with scale length. Holm and Benjamini-Hochberg must clear a floor linear in the number of comparisons. The Westfall-Young rule is the exception, in which neither sample size nor item count sets a floor on the iteration count. Its iterations are set by calibration and reproducibility, with a floor of 400 and a recommendation of 1000 to 2000 for a final analysis.

One conclusion of the earlier paper is confirmed and extended. Johansson [-@johansson_detecting_2025] compared conditional infit with conditional outfit for dichotomous items under the interval rule and found outfit worse throughout, to the point of questioning whether it is useful for detecting misfit at all. The present study reaches the same conclusion for conditional outfit under a different decision rule, the Westfall-Young corrected p-value at $B$ = 1000, and adds polytomous items, where infit again detected more misfit in every condition studied. Extending the comparison to polytomous items matters because the two formats differ in how much information each item carries, which is the same reason misfit severity has to be calibrated on the infit scale rather than on the generating parameters.

Two things are added rather than confirmed. Outfit is not miscalibrated under the corrected p-value, so its weakness is a matter of power and not of error control, and the reason for that weakness is now visible. Outfit is the more variable statistic under a true model, and its variability grows with distance from the person mean, so the items outfit is conventionally recommended for are the ones it handles worst.

## Detection at the anchored misfit level

The misfit levels used here were calibrated against real item fit values rather than chosen to be clearly detectable, and detection is correspondingly modest. With the nine phq9-derived items and a single misfitting item at $\rho$ = .85, the Westfall-Young rule detected the misfit in `r dwy("phq9", 250, 1)`% of replications at $n$ = 250 and `r dwy("phq9", 150, 1)`% at $n$ = 150, reaching `r dwy("phq9", 1000, 1)`% only at $n$ = 1000. These are the numbers for the best of the four rules. The interval rule at $w$ = .999 was lower still.

Two misfitting items are harder than one, not easier. When the off-target item q8 was made to misfit alongside q5, detection of q5 at $n$ = 250 fell from `r dwyi("phq9", 250, 1, 5)`% to `r dwyi("phq9", 250, 2, 5)`%, and q8 itself was detected in `r dwyi("phq9", 250, 2, 8)`% of replications. The same pattern appeared in the 15-item set, where a single misfitting item was detected in `r dwy("sim15", 250, 1)`% of replications at $n$ = 250 against an average of `r dwy("sim15", 250, 3)`% when three items misfit. Items that share a secondary dimension partly mask each other, because the person estimates they are evaluated against are themselves contaminated by the misfit.

The practical consequence is that at $n$ = 250 or below, an item fit analysis that flags nothing is weak evidence that nothing is wrong. This reinforces the importance of using multiple methods to evaluate item fit, especially with smaller sample sizes.

## Extension to local dependence

Nothing in these decision rules is specific to item fit. Any statistic whose cutoff is drawn from the same parametric bootstrap can be handled the same way, as long as a null distribution is generated separately for each comparison. Yen's $Q_3$ residual correlations [@yen_effects_1984] are the clearest case, since every item pair has its own expected distribution under the fitted model and simulation-based critical values for $Q_3$ have been derived before [@christensen_critical_2017]. A study of simulation-based cutoffs for evaluating local dependence with $Q_3$ residuals is in preparation.

One result carries over immediately. The number of comparisons grows quadratically with the number of items, so a 15-item scale gives 105 pairs and a 20-item scale gives 190. By @eq-bhfloor, the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure then cannot flag a single standout pair below `r bhf(105)` and `r bhf(190)` iterations respectively, which requires significant computation time. Holm has the same floor. The reachability requirement of the Westfall-Young step-down does not move, since it does not depend on the number of comparisons, and a false discovery rate criterion is therefore likely to be a poor fit for pairwise statistics such as $Q_3$. Whether the step-down's calibration and stability hold with 105 or 190 comparisons is a separate question for that study, as is subset pivotality, since residual correlations that share items are close to the case of Ferreira's [-@ferreiraMethodsTestingSmall2024] Example 2, in which the condition fails.

# Limitations

Misfit was induced by two mechanisms only. Multidimensionality is used throughout, and the mechanism check reported alongside the rule comparisons replaces it with random responding at matched infit. Other mechanisms, such as local dependence and genuine variation in item discrimination, were not examined.

Each replication is a single pass through the data. No study simulates the iterative workflow in which a flagged item is removed and the remaining items reanalyzed, which would be the practical use scenario. The error rates reported here are the rates for one analysis, and the procedures control the FWER when all items fit but not when some misfit. The iterative workflow is the practical response to that, and its error rates are the most important open question. Repeated testing across removal rounds is a further source of multiplicity that the corrections studied here do not address, and quantifying it would require a design in which the item set changes between rounds.

The scope is narrow in further respects. The item sets had 5, 9, 15, and 20 items, so @eq-fwer is verified in that range and not for longer instruments, where the joint recommendation in @tbl-recommendations extrapolates to 30 items without simulation support. The comparison between conditional infit and conditional outfit held the decision rule and the iteration count fixed, at the Westfall-Young p-value with $B$ = 1000, so it establishes an ordering at the recommended settings rather than across the design that the infit results span, and it concerns conditional outfit, not the unconditional outfit that some software reports. Of the FWER procedures, only the Westfall-Young step-down and Holm were compared, and no resampling-based false discovery rate procedure was included. Joint studentization was evaluated in the dichotomous null conditions only. Every study used $\alpha$ = .05, and while the relations themselves are general in $\alpha$, the reported rates and the calibration of the 400-iteration floor are not, so an analyst working at a different level would have to redo @tbl-recommendations and could not assume that 400 iterations still calibrates. And the anchored misfit levels were calibrated against a single instrument, which fixes the anchor to one empirical reference point rather than to a survey of what analysts encounter. That instrument has an unusual configuration, with two items far above the person mean, and the stylised 15-item set is the only regular configuration it is compared with. Matching on mean infit, finally, does not make different misfit mechanisms equivalent, as the mechanism check shows. Replication counts differ between the studies, and the Monte Carlo error of each estimate is reported in @tbl-mcse.

A practical limit shows up at the short end, and it concerns the bootstrap rather than the bound. Five polytomous items with four response categories imply fifteen threshold parameters, and at $n$ = 250 `r drop5$n_bad` of the `r format(drop5$n_all, big.mark = " ")` bootstraps run in that study produced no usable p-value at all, their simulated statistics having too little variance to studentize by. This did not occur at $n$ = 600, nor anywhere in the studies with 9 items or more. It is rare enough to be a curiosity rather than an obstacle, but a five-item scale at a small sample is where the procedure starts to strain, and nothing here establishes how it behaves below that.

# Reproducibility

```{r repro-prep}
#| include: false
sims    <- list(s_conv, s_grid, s_poly, s_stab, s_mech, s_stat, s_short)
n_cells <- sum(vapply(sims, function(x) x$own_cells %||% nrow(x$grid), numeric(1)))
n_hours <- sum(vapply(sims, function(x) x$own_min %||% x$elapsed_min, numeric(1))) / 60
```

Everything needed to reproduce this paper is in the repository at `r repo_url`, which contains the manuscript source, the simulation code, and the cached simulation results.

The manuscript is written as a Quarto document [@Allaire_Quarto_2026]. Every number reported in the body, including those in the figures and tables, is computed at render time from the cached results rather than transcribed, so the reported values cannot drift from the data behind them. The abstract is the one exception: Quarto evaluates the document metadata before the code that loads the caches, so the few figures quoted there are typed and were checked against the body by hand. Rendering the manuscript reproduces the whole paper in seconds without rerunning any simulation.

The studies are in `simulations/`, each writing its results to an `.rds` file beside it, apart from the two dichotomous studies, which were rerun for the revision with fresh data in every replication and are in `rev1/` (`fresh_rerun.R`). The original master-dataset versions of those two studies remain in `simulations/` for comparison. Three further scripts hold the calibration scans that fix the misfit levels, two of which the manuscript reads directly for @tbl-calibration and for the five-item calibration in the Method. Shared code, including the data generators and the plot theme, is in `R/helpers.R`. The seven studies comprise `r format(n_cells, big.mark = " ")` design cells and took about `r sprintf("%.0f", n_hours)` hours to run on ten M4 cores. Each study uses a resumable runner. Design cells are keyed on the columns of the design grid, results are checkpointed to disk after every chunk, and cells already present in the cache are skipped, so raising a replication count and rerunning computes only the new cells. Seeds are deterministic functions of the design cell rather than of the execution order, which means any single cell can be reproduced on its own without running the study that contains it.

All results were produced with R 4.6.1 [@r2026] and `easyRasch2` [@johanssonEasyRasch2PsychometricAnalysis2026], under versions 1.1.0 and 1.1.1 and, for the two dichotomous studies, 1.4.0. That package computes conditional item fit through `iarm` 0.4.3 [@mueller_iarm_2022] and estimates item parameters by conditional maximum likelihood with `psychotools` 0.7.6 [@zeileis_psychotools_2026]. The multidimensional dichotomous data were generated with `eRm` 1.0.10 [@mair_extended_2007], the polytomous data with the generators in `easyRasch2`, and the highest density intervals computed with `ggdist` 3.3.3 [@ggdist2025]. The phq9 data used to calibrate misfit severity are included in `easyRasch2`.

# Use of large language models

Large language models were used in preparing this work. The author designed the studies, decided which conditions to run and which results to report, verified the code and the reported values, and is responsible for all content including any errors.

A large language model was used in an agentic coding environment to write and revise the simulation code, to run the studies, and to produce the tables and figures from the cached results. It was also used to draft and revise manuscript text against an outline and instructions specified by the author, and to check the drafted text against the cached results.

Two features of the setup are relevant to assessing that use. Every value reported in the text, tables, and figures is computed from the cached simulation results when the manuscript is rendered, rather than being transcribed, so no reported number depends on a model or human correctly copying it. The simulation code, the cached results, and the manuscript source are all in the accompanying repository at `r repo_url`, so any reported quantity can be recomputed independently of the process that produced it.
